div.p: MY DEAR NELLIE,

-- There seeems to be no choice in bodices beyond the pouched, and the wide, shaped belt under a holey). I have noticed that fashion is rapidly adopting all military styles and there is specially a development of the military cuirass-bolero. One I aaw was made of violet silk, tucked in straight, per- pendicular lines, the tucks alternating with rows of fancy passementerie. Small black velvet bow!: appeared to join the sections of the bolero, but there were, in reality, no sections, and the fasten- ings were to be found under the central strip of passementerie insertion. The cuirass was slung across the shoulders with bands of black velvet. The chemisette and tops of the sleeves were white or paler mauve tucked silk. Fine tuckings appeared again upon the wide, cup-shaped cuffs that fell over the hands. The rest of the sleeves was made of plain mauve silk. The belt was black crepe-de-chine, with fringed ends, fastening at the left under a buckle or cairngorm.

The war seems to have impressed itself upon fashionable headgear. A chapeau, which I had the pleasure of seeing yesterday was the "petit corporal" hat in net over satin, with the front turned upwards and sideways to show the hair. There was another model, which curved up at one side, dipped in front and at the back, and at the other side drooped also as if to caress the hair. Small flowers are attractive, dainty roses and star eyed forget-me-nots, but to many of the flowers that bloom in the milliners' shop it is difficult to give a name. They are pretty, except when they are of the so-called pastel shades. It is not in art to copy a rain-drenched blossom, and that is the only pastel one nature knows. Another pretty hat was formed of drawn and pleated crinoline, -wired and bent into the picturesque shape, loose tulle strings fastening in a knot under the chin. The brim, curiously enough, was lined with black velvet, exactly opposite to the ordinary employ- ment of these materials. It is very easy to trim a hat at home in these days, as very little else is required than clusters of flowers and foliage, and trails of leaves.

This summer will be remembered for a very long time by reason of the great number of persons in mourning. Though the etiquette of mourning is not nearly so stringent as it used to be, nor the duration so long, yet he rules are observed with some strictness. For instance, with crape on the gown no white is admissible, save the line of white crape under the brim of the widow's bonnet, and her white batiste collar and cuffs. These latter, a comparatively recent innovation, originated in England. Glossy materials, like satin and glace silk, are also incompatible with crape. Jet, even of the most brilliant kind, is worn with crape, though seldom for the first three months of very deep mourning. Chiffon and silk muslin are very largely used in mourning, whether in combination with crape or alone. Some unusually attractive materials are prepared this season for mourning wear. Grenadines, whether plain or patterned, gauzes of the finest and silkiest sort, crepons of different designs, among which round spots in black or white seem to be the favourite, canvas plain or striped, some glossy with the silky sheen of flax, and silk crepes, which differ from crepe-de- chine only in being thicker than the latter material.

A dress I have just seen is in printed foulard twill, patterned with mauve and rose hydrangeas. The skirt is set in pleats, the upper part simulat- ing a panier. Round the bodice are rows of black ribbon velvet, resembling a bolero in shape, gathered into a bunch on the left side. The hat is trimmed with hydrangeas and black velvet. Another dress is a pretty walking costume in blue cloth, opening over a petticoat in two shades of cerise. The bolero fastens over a shirt of cerise silk, with revers of red cloth, and is strapped across at the lower edge with gold buckles.
Your loving JENNIE.

"WOMEN'S CHAT."

It would probably surprise many people if it were known how much the Queen has given from her privet.? purse to aid works of charity. On the occasion of her visit to Dublin she gave £l,OOO for the benefit of the poor of that city, to say nothing of the numerous oth r donations and presents of which the aggregate value must have amounted to a considerable sum. Another more recent gift is the donation of 500 guineas to the Mansion House Fund, for the relief of the sufferers by the fire at Ottawa. During the past few days, Her Majesty has sent her annual contribution of a hundred guineas to the Seamen's flespital Society, and the fact has transpired that this is the 63rd gift of that amount I which the Society has received from her since ner acces- sion, making a total of £6,615. As an illustration cf how little public interest is taken in Indian affairs, it is stated that the appeal for the Famine Fund at Colchester is a failure. Pun& opinion in this country would seem to be relying upon the Government of India and the Government at home, icing all that is necessary, and fortunately for the starving millions of Indies, this reli- ance appears to he fully justified. Teem is neverthe- less ample scope for public assistance. Colchester is one of the pelt; cipel towns of Essex, with a population of 35.600, hut only £69 has been raised, and at a meeting of the Corporation the other cay, the Mayor announced that he would close the fund, and have nothing more to do with it. Not a single clergs man it sei me, and net a single noccor, subscribed a penny t wards the £69, though ne less than two lawyers name forward and vindicatad the reputation of the legal profession for charity. The hospital ship Maine has done splendid work in bringing home the wounded. While giving them all the advantages of skilled nursing, and the best medical treatment, it has relieved the advance and hale hospitals in South Africa, of the pressure upon their accommoda• tion. The report ef the work performed on board is in every way satisfactory, wad gives nothing hut un stinted praise to the women forming the nursing sniff. It is no reflection upon their services, that it has been decided to carry male nurses only in future. Some people may be disposed to connect this decision with some recent remarks of Mr. Trevea Nothing how- ever would be further from the truth. In the first place no one Ism a higher epinien of the women who devote their lives to nursing.and ef the iuveluable services they render in ministering to the sick. What Mr. Treves said was directed against those society women who make nursing and hospital visiting, a pretence for their own amusement and excitement. On board the Maine, it is thought that better results will be obtained by carrying only male nurses, because what with sea sickness and the necessarily cramped accommodation it is not the . place where women'a work can be turned to best advantage. There is a very general impre3sion even among quali- fied nurses, that there is more nouriehment in " beef- tea " than any other form of food. This, in some res- pects, is quite a mistake, and it is not incorrect to say, there is no nourishment in what is called " strong beef- tea." It is more properly speaking a stimulant, and when combined with a certain amcunt of solids, or other elements necessary to support life, it is invaluable for the sick and weakly, but by itself, or in over pro- portion,it affords little or to benefit to the system. Any- one who tried to live upon beef-'.ea alone would quickly die of starvation, because its chemical composition is minus some of the elements essential to life and health. This is often over'ooked in nursing the sick, and when it is suppes-d that the patient is "Joins; well " upon beef-tea, it may be the case that he or she is really starv- ing upon it. The new sunshade with detachable cover, is indeed a boon awl a blessing ts women with limited dress allow- ance. These covers can be adjusted in two or three minutes, and instead of having to purchase a sunshade with each coetume, one is sufficient, a new cover only being necessary with eech frock, In travelling too, we shall find this particular idea a highly satisfactory one. with our wraps and umbrella, we can strap the one handle and frame, and stow away all coven in our portmanteau. Irish poplin is being widely worn, and promises to continua in favour. Toe majsrity of our Princesses are very fond of the fabric, especially the Duchesses of Con- Naught, York, and Fife, and Princess Vietoria of Wales. Her Majesty purchased many lengths of poplin during her visit to the Emerald Isle, exquisite specimens, the several lengths for personal wear being of course, in black. White drill was somewhat too popular last summer for coat and skirt costumes, to appeal to the conclusive ones this, but coloured drills .will be much VI evidence among well-dressed woneen, elaborately stitched of course. The best frocks of this description show white stitchings, and a white silk vest ; a white silk shirt, much tucked, beiog provided to take the place of the coat and vest,when the warm hays coins to stay. No one ever hears of took pie, though at one time it was considered something of a delicacy, and this is the month when it was usual to kill off the young ones. It is the only kind of sheeting available at this time of year,and sometimes it used to be the Squire's party who went forth on this errand, but more often it was left to a number of village worthies to indulge in the sport. Possibly this still goes on in the country, though it is quite certain that rook-pie is not such a favourite dish as it wa.s in the days of Mr. Pickwick. Many people object to waging war upon birds of such a sociable dis- position as the rooks, but unless they were periodically thinned they would probably become a great nuisance. In some parts of the country, especially in Scotland, the farmers have been waging a war of extermination against the rooks, though many believe they do more good than harm. There is this difference betweeu gardening and house- hold work, while one is compulsory, the other is usually a pleasure. or at. least a matter of choice. That is per- haps why labour saving appliances have never made so much progress in the garden, as they have in the house, or on the farm, and there is little in fact beyond the lawn mower and the garden hose.which modern icgenu- ity has discovered to lighten garden work. The condition in which those two useful articles are now discovered, depends much upon the care taken of them during the winter. There is nothing so cheap in the end as the better qualities of hose. The " Me rry weather " easily admits of repeir,—an item indeed worthy of our con- sideration.

ESTABLISHED 1866.
CRANE AND SONS, LIMITED, LIVERPOOL. THE PROPOSED HOSPITAL AT SAN KEY.

The question of the proposed erection of a small-pox hospital at Sankey by tee Warrington Corporation was the subject of discussion at a meeting of the Great Sankey Parish Council on Monday evening. Mr. Thomas Halton who presided said the members would remember that at tho last meeting he gave notice of his intention to draw attention to this question. He understeod that in the first instance it was contemplated to effect a union between Warrineton, St. Helens and Widnes, and erect a hospital for tha thre. towns,bnt St. Helens and Widnes withdrew, as as as natural seeing that the proposee site was so unsuitatle. It was not necessary just now to go into details, and all be wished to know was whether the meeting cousidered it desirable to call a ratepayers' meeting or whether the Clerk should at once be instructed to write to the L.cal Government Board aeking if the members of the Council could have an interview with their inspector when he came to inspect the site. Their Clerk c.iuld also say that they had the strongest objection t) the propos.' of the Warrington Corporation,not because it was a small-cox ho.pital they intended to erect, but bnause the site was unsuitable. They had no power to object so long as the Corporation chose an isolated site, but this site was not isolated. Teere were two farms within a quarter of a mile from it, and several eottaees and houses not half a mile away. The Clerk (Mr. J. Smith), said it was areu id that the hospital need not he isolated. Still it was SoME thing in their objection. The question of soil and sub-soil and seerering might be mentioned. The Chairman vale the Corporation bad two other places on their hands which were purchased seine time ' ago, and he believed the Health Csmmittee 'sad unanim- ously selected one site for tlse erEction of a small-pox hospital. They had been led to understand that plans had been prepared. Whether the Local Government Board considered the site was not sufficiently isolated or the clay land with surface water rendered it unsuitable be could not say, but those objections could be clearly urged in regard to the land at Sankey. He thought they as a Council should be fully prepared to oppose the pro- posed erection of this hespitel, and they had many grounds of objection. The Sankey people were not the only people aggrieved, for he was assured by gentlemen who lived in the neighbourhoed of Peaketla that they would give the Council every support. The best policy at the present moment would be to instruct the clerk to writ. to the Local Government Board. The Corporation would lose no time in purchasing this site after obtain- ing the sanction of the Local Government Board. If the Local Government Board ordered a public inquiiy ob• j,ction would br made to the proposal of the Cerporation not only by the Council but by several landewners in the district. There would not be time in which to call a ratepayers' meeting, and he could not bring the matter before the Rural Council for another fortnight. He therefore proposed that the Clerk be instructed to write to the Local Government Board asking for a public in qntry. Mr. loseph K.lshaw se:one-led. He thought it the wisest proposal, and they would have the support of the landowners. _ . .

The Clerk said that he wrote the following letter on May 4th, to Mr. J. C. Sutton, clerk to the Rural District Council :—At the annual meeting of the above Parisi Courcil I was instructed to write you rsspecting the pro- posed erection of a small-pox hospital near Lingley Green in the township of Great Sankey by the Corporation of Warrington, and it was resolved that Mr. Halton, a member of the Rural District Council, be authorizei to bring the matter before your next meeting with a view to obtaining the assistance of your Council in opposing such proposal. My Parish Council have no hesitation in stating that the proposed site is altogether unsuitable, and that a sewage scheme would be necessitated together with an extension of gas and water mains. The township would thus be saddled with an extreniely heavy burden and the present development of the parish would un- , dciebtedly be brought to a stand. My Council contend I that there are other sites more advantageous in every 1 way,and they will be pleased if your Council will strongly oppose any itrth erection on the site referred to. Some discussion followed. The Clerk thought tr.at St. Helens and Widnes bad withdrawn from the scheme because they did not ap- prove of the site. The Chairman : I think that is so. Mr. J. li.lshaw : The place is not isolated at all. The Chairman said he knew for a positive fact that the plans for a hospital on the other side of Orford were passed two years since. The Health Committee were unanimous in selecting the site. Mr. Bilshaw said the land at Sankey ran down to the brook. The site was very unsuitable. The Chsirman said he was determined to have the matter thrashed out to the bitter end. Be did not object to a small-pox hospital in itself, but he strongly objected to one on such a site. It was one of the worst places that could be f3und for sanitation. Mr. Kilshaw : They will not get a fall for their sewage. The Clerk said the river at flood tide was level with this land. The r.ainn was then put to the meeting and carried.

HALF A CENTURY
THE ;.,XAIVIINL'iz, FRIDAY, MAY ii 1900

remember, and lnese I mu, remember, old man, your kindness, your cheeriness, your hearty comradeship, you,- sublime altruism, your manli- ness. Good-bye, Barnard, old man. You have been a good friend to me, a better friend to me than you will ever know. Take care of yourself; the world can't spare such fellows as you. Ah, you laugh 1 It is little use me telling you to take care of yourself, I see; you'll always be caring for others. Good-bye, old mai), and yet not for long, I hope. We shall meet again. I'll write to you often."
.—The train had drawn up and Steve stepped aboard. "Good-bye, my friend," said Barnard, feelingly. "Keep a good heart. Good-bye my lad," and with hearty hand-grip the friends parted.
The Braemar Castle was nearing her last port of call. The Natal coast with the low hills beyond could clearly be discerned. In a few hours Durban would be reached.
- Ella Rayburn was seated alone on the after-deck, her erstwhile pale face lighted up with the warm rays of the setting sun, which was Lfast dipping behind the western hills.

Ella had become very moody and contemplative of-late, vastly different to her old gay, thoughtless self. Since that terrible morning when she saw a distracted man rush ashore from the vessel at Cape- town she had become fretful and humorsome, until Percival was well-nigh driven to desperation by her ^-nduct. They had quarrelled every day since, and .ach time when the wordy combat had ended Percival had adjourned to the bar and drunk to excess. He was now lying in his cabin helplessly inebriated. Ella dreaded the moment when he would again come to her. Oh, what a terrible position she was placed in! She was about to enter a strange land without a friend to help her. So violent and threatening had Percival become of late that she feared to trust herself ashore with him. Yet she would have to go. She had promised to be his wife. Oh, it was distracting! She looked listlessly on this strange land, on the "wattle and daub" huts of the natives which dotted the hill slopes. This country had now no interest for her. A low, sandy shore stretched away to the right, while on the left was a bold, tree-covered bluff surmounted by a lighthouse. The town of Durban, situated a mile inland, with the well-wooded Berea in the background, presented a pleasing picture to the eyes of the voyagers. The night shadows were falling ere the Braemar Castle was docked. , Ella and her tipsy lover stood on deck behind the crowd of passengers, impatiently waiting to go ashore. "Is the luggage all right ? " she asked Percival. "Yes, I s'pect so. Steward knows about it. I've told him," he answered, jerkily. "Well, I must have my trunk if we're going ashore to-night," she said. "Of course we're going ashore to-night. Think we're going to stop on this ship for ever? Ought to have got off at Capetown, instead of coming on to this fever-stricken, benighted place." She left him and went to ask one of the stewards to see that her trunk was put on the quay. "Where are you? Ah ! If she tries to give me the slip now, I'll—" "Where shall I send Miss Rayburn's trunk to, Mr. Percival ? " a steward asked, coming up to him. "Send it to—to— Which is the best hotel here, steward ? " "The Cosmopolitafl,s a good hotel, sir." "Send it to the Cosmopolitan then. Say, you'll send mine with it, too ? "

"All right, sir." Ella now rejoined him and together they stepped ashore. A crowd of ricksha boys rushed up. Selecting one of the vehicles Percival ordered his companion to "step in.,, She quietly obeyed and he was about to seat him- self beside her when the Zulu spoke. "I conna, boss, I conna." "Eh, what d'ye mean ? " cried Percival, not comprehending the meaning of the words but perceiving by the man's actions and gestures that hewished to prevent him from entering the vehicle.

"I conna, I conna," repeated the ricksha boy, "He means that you cannot join the lady," said European standing by. "There is not room for two." "Isn't there? Is that what the nigger means? I'll shew the black rascal how he should treat a • gentleman." He rushed viciously at the native, but the agile fellow quickly skipped aside and , avoided the onslaught. Ella jumjied from the ricksha. "Ralph! Ralph!" she cried. "Don't bother. Come along, here's a cab." After considerable difficulty she induced him to enter the larger vehicle and they drove off, the ricksha boy running alongside jabbering excitedly. As they alighted at the Cosmopolitan Hotel in the centre of the town the Zulu, still loudly chattering, came up, gesticulating wildly. Ella gave him a couple of shillings, whereupon the delighted fellow ran off, leaping and prancing , between the shafts of his ricksha. "Are you going to be the boss ? " Percival asked, seeing what Ella had done. "Yes, until you're sober," she answered, as she paid the cab-driver, "Sober 1" he exclaimed, wrathfully. "Are you insulting me now? Sober! You see a rascally black thief insult me, and you give him money to go away quietly, then you insult me." She walked towards the hotel entrance and he followed behind, fuming and cursing. "Sober ! By Heavens, I'll shew her how sober • „ am! Sober enough not to be bossed by her." He walked unsteadily to the office, and, addressing the clerk, said curtly: "We want rooms. "Yes, sir." "For self and wife." Ella, who had come up, started at his words. "Yes, sir. What name, pleabe ? " "Percival, Mr. and Mrs. Percival." "Ralph I" Ile heeded her not, but turned abruptly and stepped into an adjoining-room. For a moment she hesitated whether to follow him or leave the hotel at once. He called her by name and she went to him. Then the door closed with a loud bang. "Sit down," he said, imperiously. . She looked at his angry face then obeyed. "Take off your hat and things," he said, in the same commanding .tone. "D'ye hear ? " as she sat motionless. "I am not. your slave,":she said, quietly, but with telling emphasis. "Not my slave, you say? By Heavens! But you are, body and soul! You've sold yourself to me, d'ye hear ? " With an impatient gesture she rose to her feet, and was walking towards the door when he stopped her. "Let me go," she said, in a quiet voice: "You are not yourself to-night." "Not myself, eh ?" he roared. "I don't know wnat I'm doing or saying, eh? That's what you mean. Think I'm a drunken fool, don't you? But I'm sober enough for you, Miss Rayburn. Sit down! I'll not let you go," he said, as she tried to reach the door. "Miss Rayburn, eh? But you're Mrs. Percival now, d'ye hear? You heard what I said to the clerk. Mrs. Percival. That's a nicer name than your own. Say good-bye to Miss Rayburn now, for ever. You are mine now, body and soul. D'ye hear? You're my devoted slave. I've been yours long enough; now you'll be mine." He paused, and paced about the room excitedly, then began afresh. fine life I've led this last week with you and your sulky, saucy humours. You're to blame for this. You've driven me to it. Why were you ever- lastingly weeping and wailing like a simpering, moping fool? This is nice payment for all my kindness and care." She regarded him with a contemptuous glance, which he was quick to observe. "Oh, you can affect to be disgusted with me. That's your style. You've pretended to be dis- gusted before. You look well as the injured maiden, you do. You are a much-wronged .saint, you are. Why don't you try to be as amiable and pleasing as you were, say a month ago? But, no, you'd rather be a simpering wailer or a howling termagant. . . . Why don't you speak? Why 4on't you say something ? " 3 I've nothing to say,' she answered, 'quietly, as indeed she had not at that moment. To speak to him whilst he was in this frenzy she knew would be futile. "Nothing to say, eh? But you'd enough to say a few minutes ago, when you said I wasn't sober. You'd enough to say yesterday, wheli I asked you to be reasonable and friendly, and you flared up, and said you wouldn't be any man's mistress. Mistress, eh You would be master now if you could; wouldn't you, my lady? But not yet, my lady. You'll be my slave. I've bought you, and

div.head: (Copyright.) STEVE, THE OUTLANDER.
div.p: (Copyright.) STEVE, THE OUTLANDER.
Dv ARTHUR LAYCOCK Author of "The Young Gaffer," "Seaside Sketches.°
"Lancashire Sketches," &c.

CHAPTER XXIII. Capetown Park is the favourite rendezvous of new arrivals, out-of-works, and casuals of all classes. When these people are tired of sight- seeing or street-loafing, or vain searching for work, when the scorching sun becomes unendurable to them, they flock to the park and recline on the benches or 101 l upon the sweet, refreshing patches

of green-sward. Steve passed by the fountain and entered a shady glade where, on one of the seats, sat a man poring over a railway time-table. As Steve seated himself at the further end of the form the man looked up for a second, then, with an amused smile, turned his attention again to the time-table. "This beats Bradshaw," he said at length, turn- ing to Steve, who was quietly munching his grapes, "Whoever it be who compiles these railway guides is a genius. He beats Bradshaw hollow." Steve moved towards him. _

_ "Perhaps I can help you," he said. "Where do you want to get to ? "Bloemfontein. Hulloa Excuse me, but aren't you the friend who spoke to me yesterday down on the quay ? " Steve looked confused as he recognised the tall passenger. "I am." "I thought so. Did you find your friend?" It was an embarrassing question. Steve quailed and his face became suddenly pale. "No, I—l did not." His features twitched nervously as he strove to control himself. "Ah I I see. You've been badly hit, friend," said Barnard, sympathetically. "fm sorry I've upset you." "It's all right," said Steve, manfully, his voico betraying intense emotion. "I have been badly hit." "And by a woman," said Barnard, "I know." "You know ? " cried Steve, excitedly. "What do you know ? " "That the girl you asked me about had deceived you. I could have told you yesterday when you started so as I told you she was travelling first-
class." "Did you know the man ? " "Not intimately; only as a fellow-passenger."
"And his name?"

"Percival.," "A stranger, an utter stranger," Steve muttered to himself. Then, as a new thought occurred to him: "What was his Christian name?" "Ralph, I believe." "Ralph Percival," slowly repeated Steve. Then, after a pause: "Was he of middle-height, dark- complexion, hair grey about the ears ? " yes.” "About thirty-five years of age?"

yes.” "It is he! Curse him! I knew it! I knew it! I felt it the first night I sailed from England, felt that he was drawing her into his power. I have felt it ever since. He'll drag her into hell! Curse him! I could kill him!' Barnard looked pityingly on the frenzied lover, who clenched his fists convulsively in his uncon- trolable wrath. Presently Steve calmed down. "What have I been saying, eh? Don't think anything of it. I've been badly upset ever since. I hardly know what I am doing. Then they talked together quietly, the elder man by his kindly speech and sympathetic manner drawing out from Steve all that was best and noblest in him. When they left the park an hour later they were sworn friends. "We are comrades in misfortune," said Barnard, who had told a little of his own life troubles. "Let us be comrades in good fortune so far as life yet holds good fortune for us. lam doomed to die in a few years, my medical friends tell me. I have been a medical student myself and know that they speak truly. In England lives a good woman, an all-sacrificing woman, who would have been my wife to-day if I had said the word. But I loved her too well to blight her life, to transmit to her— and may be to others—the fell disease with which .I am afflicted. We parted. Heaven knows how I I try not to think of it. I try to think that lam in a new world now where I must endeavour to make the best of the few, short years yet left to me. If in my brief time I can give happiness, joy, comfort to but a few fellow-travellers on the journey I shall cross the bar happily, meet death with a smile on my face." Stephen Hart was deeply impressed with his newly-found friend. How different was he to the men with whom he had lately been associated, who thought not a others but only of self. As Steve contemplated this man of big heart and wide sympathies, he felt somewhat ashamed of himself; felt how unworthy was he to be regarded as friend by such a noble, unselfish man. 'My life has had but one central thought—Ella," he said to himself; "For her I have toiled and slaved, for her I have hoarded up gold. Yes, I have thought much of gold. I have dreamt of it. At times it has driven out thoughts of aught else. Yes, Ella has then been forgotten, although 'twas for her that I first engaged in this grasping work for gold. I sent her a paltry twenty-five pounds when I might well have sent her four times that amount which I had saved, but hoped to give her as a wedding present. I've been greedy, I've been selfish, I believe. And I've only just discovered this now that I have come in contact with a totally unselfish man." That night the two friends left Capetown for the north. Steve, who had previously mastered the intricacies of Cape Government Railway _time- tables, soon overcame the difficulties therein which had troubled Barnard go much. Both of the travellers had secured sleeping berths, and, after a short chat, turned in and were soon wrapped in slumber. Steve had agreed to accompany his companion to Bloemfontein and there remain until Barnard had succeeded in pro- curing accommodation at one or another of the Free State farms in the neighbourhood. A pleasant journey through slightly undulating country brought them at length to their destination, a snug, substaintial-looking dwelling near the river, and almost surrounded by trees. The two friends remained at this place for a week, and at the end of that period : Barnard informed Steve that he had decided to take up permanent residence on the farm. "One place is pretty near as good as another for me," he said. "It will make little difference where I stay, but this place will do as well as any, p;rhaps better than most. The boss' is a good, genial fellow, his wife is kindly and motherly, and the rest of the family appear to be a decent lot. I think I shall get .on very well with them." "But what about all the other boarders ? " Steve asked. "They won't be very bright companions, will they ? " "No, poor chaps,, it's hardly likely they will. All imagers, ' r Understand, in various stages of phthisis. It is.hardly likely in their condition that they will be very bright, that's all the more reason why / should be. ,With all my ailments I've been blessed with a cheery disposition, thank God. Ah, yes," he continued, speaking with fervour. "I can find plenty to do among these poor fellows. I'll cheer 'em up and help them in many a way. Some of them are not so bad, and, with my profes- sional knowledge of our common complaint, I think I can restore some of these doubtfuls 'to sound health again. If -I can't cure myself I believe I can help to cure them. At least I'll try." ' Steve marvelled at his companion's self-abnega- tion. No thought of self, no thought of living through the weary' days in company with these poor, spiritless "lungers " ; sickly fellows all, who nibbled gingerly at their food and were depressing in the extreme to a hale, hearty man like Steve. Barnard thought only of making the lot of his unfortunate comrades brighter and better. "A noble fellow, a veritable God-man," said Steve, as he reflected on his companion's sterling qualities. He remained another jeek at the farm, then, accompanied by Barnard, proceeded to Bloemfontein. At the railway station they liad their last chat. "And where are you going to now ? " asked Barnard. "I itarcely know," Steve answered. "Some- where in the Transvaal, though where I can't exactly say yet. I'll not go back to Johannesburg, at any rate, for a time. Perhaps I'll roam amongst the burghers, visit the farms, do a bit of transport- riding, or anything that turns' up. I can ride, drive, shoot, and do most kinds of mining work. 1 shall tumble into something or other. I'm not 'particular what I do or where I go. I want to forget some thins. Other things I want to

div.p: uy heaven, 111 nave you ioa.ve mulling to say, eh? but you'd much to say yesterday, Nv!ten you said I promised to marry you. Marry you! I! should be a fool! AS if .I had ever thought of warn ing_you." _ . _

S'tie titsvituperation. might have continue much longer had not a waiter disturbed him in his Fiery harangue. 'Supper is ready, sir. °' "Come along ! " he said, in a changed tone as the man left the room. "Come along, and let's forget all this. You have irritated me. You shouldn't have ssid I was drunk. Never mind; let's be friends. Come to supper! I shall be all right to-morrow, when the drink's out of me, though I'm sober now. You'll be all right too, then. Come, go upstairs and take your things off, and we'll have supper, and be better tempered with each other. You'll forget all that I've said to-morrow. Sa shall I. Come along, now!" He opened tip door and they passed into the hall. A chambermaid came forward and conducted Elle to her apartment. Percival remained at the foot of the staircase.

"Better stop to see she doesn't give me the slip," he said to himself. "Oh, she'd do it, if she got half a chance I was a fool to rave at her so, but curse her! she's so exasperating! Ah She's safe for to-night anyhow!" He lighted a cigar and walked towards the entrance.

"Supper quite ready, sir," said a coloured waitew bowing obsequiously. "Yes, coming ii a moment, Sambo." He looked back impatiently towards the staircase. "Confound these women and their fixings ! " he muttered. "She's a deuce of a while ! "

At that precise moment Ella was cautiously peep- ing down the staircase. There was no chance of escape that way. She looked down a long passage leading to the rear premises. Surely there would be stairs at the end. Yes, a Kaffir servant was descending there now ! She hurried forward, and, to her joy, saw a narrow staircase. She ran down it, and to the astonishment of several coloured domestics, rushed through the kitchen, and passed out at the back door. She soon gained the street, and hurrying forward came to a wide, well-lighted thoroughfare. A tramcar was slowly jingling along. Hot and flurried, she jumped aboard it and was carried up West-street, in the direction of the Berea. Her hair was dishevelled, and from the curious looks of her fellow-passengers, she judged that her appearance was altogether noticeable. She therefore dropped off at the first stage. Before her was a clean, quiet-looking boarding-house. "Thank God!" she exclaimed, in a suppressed whisper. "I'm safe for to-night, at any rate," and she entered the house.

div.head: CHAPTER XXIV.
div.p: CHAPTER XXIV.
Many weeks Ella Rayburn remained at the Durban boarding-house, scarce daring to venture out of doors, fearing that she might encounter the man whom she now dreaded above all others.
iqi.er,-t-r—o—ublo-us- weeks were these as she meditated on her folly and wrong-doing.

That she truly loved Steve above all other Inert on earth she knew that dreadful morning when, in anguish, she screamed as he left the ship. Ah, why did she not follow him then, as her love prompted her to? Why did she not flee from the wretch who, finding her completely in his power, sought to ruin her body and soul? She had found out too late the true character of Ralph Percival. She had found out too late her own true character. Never until now had she realised how much she loved Steve. She had thought that she had loved herself above all, but it was not so. True, she had lived for self, and self alone, these many years. But deep down in her heart was a strong, abiding love for one other, and that other Stephen Hart. And now he was lost to her for ever. Ah, well, it was too late now to repine. She must make the best of life, and live it out in this strange land for a time. For she could not think of returning to England. Return there to hear from the lips of her friends the story of her falsity to Stephen Hart ? No, she could not bear that. She would remain in this sunny land, forgotten, alone. At least she would be in the same country as Steve, and that would be some comfort to her.

Ella found that she could not remain much longer at the boarding-house. Her little stock of money had dwindled down to a few shillings. In her hurried flight from the Cosmopolitan Hotel she had, perforce, to leave behind her trunk, containing wearing apparel and many other necessaries, most of which she had been compelled to replace. Her purse had, therefore, Soon become well-nigh depleted. She would have to secure employment, and that very soon. But what could she do? Domestic work she was used to; but in this town coloured servants alone were employed for such labour. Her landlady thought she might procure a situa- tion as lady's-maid or nurse. Ella, therefore, scanned the advertisement columns of the local papers, daily, and at last came upon an item which immediately drew her close attention: "Wanted, European lady, as nurse for two children. Apply—Musgrave-road, Berea." Ella went to the place and secured the situation. Her new home, situated in the most beautiful part of the Berea, was a handsome colonial house surrounded by fair gardens, orange groves, and pine-apple and banana plantations. English roses and all kinds of beautiful flowers grew in profusion, and to Ella tha pretty spot was a veritable Eden. Here for two months she remained, content with her lot. Then, as the summer season advanced, with hot, sultry, moist days and stifling nights,, she longed for a cooler and more bracing clime. Ah, could she but be in England now, when the days . were becoming sharp and frosty. England! No! She must not think of it. Never more could she return to Dalesworth to face the scorn and contumely of the folks who knew her there and who would doubtless have heard of her folly. She had not written to relations or friends since her arrival in South Africa. On a certain afternoon in late December she was strolling along Musgrave-road with her two little charges, when the shout of a drunken man startled her. Quickly she glanced behind and saw with horror Percival, drunk and stupefied, leaning back in a ricksha. He was t a vling to the boy who was pulling him along, but the prancing Zulu, merely grinning, paid little heed to his fare. "D'ye hear, ye son of Satan Stop! Stop ! " cried Percival. 'Hi 1 Hi I Stop; there's a face I know there. Hi! You, woman! I want you!" Ella, seizing the children, hurried away. "Stop, you black rascal! Stop!" • Percival leant forward and struck the ricksha boy a violent blow in the back. The man dropped the shafts and the vehicle fell on its side, the drunken fare being hurled at full length on the road. I native policeman and several white folks ran up, and as Ella looked fearfully back, she saw Percival and the ricksha boy in the custody of the police. The next day she read an account of Percival's appearance in the police-court. He was charged with being drunk and disorderly, and further with having committed an assault on a ricksha boy. In his defence he stated that the boy was to blame for the assault, he having refused to pull up when ordered to do so. He furthermore charged the native with robbing him. "I had eighty pounds, your worship," he said, addressing the bench, "eighty, pounds when I entered that ricksha, and now I haven't got a cent." He was fined twenty shillings and costs, but, having no money to'po.y the fine, was committed to gaol for fourteen days. When Ella had read the report she decided to leave the town without further delay. "So long as he is here, I can never feel safe," she thought. "I must go far away from this place. I'll go to Johannesburg. He can't follow me there if he's no money." A week later she was in the Golden City. Hour after hour she had journeyed through uncultivated, uninhabited country, across rolling, monotonous veld, and it seemed to her that she was being borne to some spot far beyond civilisation. When she came to Johannesburg, therefore, her surprise was great. Here were all the signs of civilisation; fine, modern buildings, shops, houses, marts, wide thoroughfares, electric light, tramcars, policemen, and thousands of bustling people. This was in some respects reassurin,g, yet, as Ella roamed about these busy streets, thronged with men, mostly young, with but few women faces to cheer her, she felt intensely lonely. "Where should she go ? To whom should she go ? " she asked herself, as bhe walked along in the heat and glare of the fierce October sun. Men glanced askance at her. Some peered im- pudently into her face, others jostled her familiarly ; one or two spoke to her, but she heeded them not She became afraid and still more afraid, as, strolling down Pritchard-street, she saw women gauciil7 dressed, and with painted faces, flaunting them- selves boldly before the public gaze. Ah, she must leave this part of the town, and at Once! She mist go somewhere else. But where? To an hotel or boardinghouse? Crossing Von Brandis-square, • she came to a quieter street. Here she was out of the bustling throne. safe, from the bold. searching, meanine

glances or tne men. u ainoiestect, sae cotua WOK about for a board i g-h on se. A Dutch policeman was standing in the midcl;B of the road. She wont, to him and asked if he could direct her to a likely place. The stolid fellow, mouth half-open, stared stupidly at her 8,4 mOment, then jabbered in incomprehensible Dutcho Ella turned sadly away; she would have to ask someone else. Men passed to and fro, but she was loth to accost them. At last she espied a woman standing at the door of an adjacent house, and she went to her. "Boarding-houses ? " said the woman, in answer' to her query. "Yes, there's plenty of 'em about here. What sort do you want ? " and she smiled roguishly. Ella quickly interpreted the smile. "I want $ respectable, clean place," she said, with dignity. "Oh," returned the woman, shortly. Then as ir prompted by an afterthought, "Of course I didn't think you wanted the other sort. You'd better tri the next street." Offended and disgusted, • Ella walked away, and' turning aside, came to a narrow thoroughfare where shops and houses alternated. A boarding-houB . sign attracted her attention, and she crossed rfeh to the house. "Don't take women boarders here," said the stout landlady, regarding Ella suspiciously. "Can you recommend me to a place? " 'was tile

timid request. "No, I can't," said the woman, decisively. "I'el not going to recommend you or any other strange young woman to any place I know of, for perher/ you wouldn't suit them, or they wouldn't suit you• You'll have to try somewhere else, miss." The woman did not speak altogether unkindlY; but the way in which she shrugged her broae shoulders as she spoke made her words seer(' curiously significant to her listener. Ella becaine alarmed. Each of the two women to whom she had spoken appeared to regard her suspiciously. What could it mean? Then she remembered the gay women she had seen parading themselves. Oh, terrible thought! Could it be that she Noe regarded as being one of those abandoned creatures ? It was not unlikely. Here was a woman, alone, le the city of gold—and infamy. Throughout the long hot afternoon Ella searched in vain for a place' where she might stay. She had tea in a siu3l' restaurant in Commissioner-street, and here told one of the waitresses of her difficulty.
"You are quite alone ?' said the kirl. "Yes, and I do not know a soul in this city." "And you have come here to-day from Natal 7'' "Yes."

"Were you alone there ? " "Yes—yes," stammered Ella. Then as the girl looked keenly at her, Ella fe3 that she was again doomed by one of her own 1 "I—l'm sorry, but I don't know of any place, the girl said. The proprietor of the establishment now caw. forward. "What is it the lady wants ? ":he asked.

The waitress explained. He appeared to be greatly amused by the situy tion, which to Ella was becoming terribly serious. "Ah Oh, yes I see I " Then as he directed the waitress to attend to her duties, "Yes, I think can tell you of a suitable place." He scrawled address on a small card, and handing it to 80/ with a smile, said: I "You are certain to find accommodation there', They'll be only too glad to take in a pretty gir; ,like you." I Ella left the restaurant, blushing, as she heal the titters of the waitresses and the loud guffaws °' the vulgar proprietor. I Doubtless it was a great joke to them to see LI lonely girl in such a helpless predicament. I For a moment she felt tempted to tear up til,e card and fling the scraps in the face of the heartiTt, crowd. Then she reflected that the address wig'. be genuine. She made many inquiries for the streetti named on the card, and at length found it, ell proceeded to the house indicated. The two lowe rooms of the dwelling were lighted and the blluo drawn, for it was now dark. Ella went boldly uP to the door and pressed the electric bell. For full minute she waited ere the door was cautiouw...; opened a few inches, then a light curly head glir seen as a woman's shrill voice asked:

, "What do you want ? " I "I want lodgings, please, and—" "Come in." She was pulled into the dimly-lighted hall by th. light-haired woman, who stood regarding 11 approvingly. "You'll do, my dear. All righb Come along! " A sudden fear seized Ella. There was something so mysterious about the woman, and the house so strange that she felt all was not right. 1 She rushed to the door and tried to unfasten "Now! There! What are you doing ? " oleo the woman: "I wish to go out." "You—what? Why, didn't you just say S°l; wanted to come in? " "I did. Yes, I know, but—" "There's no 'buts' about it," said the worasof sharply. "You're here, and you've got to stoP• Claude!" A man came hurrying forward. "Seize that girl, the woman cried. The fellow rushed up to do bidding, but Ella was prepared for the attack, avv" catching up a plant-pot, hurled it with all her fore° at his head. He staggered and fell, and ilr„ woman, dashing forward, stumbled over his prostrsw body. Ella tugged and pulled at the many bolt! and latches of the door. Then a girl's arm reacht: over her shoulder and shot back a tiny bolt, and, Ella turned fearfully round, the pitying eye 01" pretty brunette looked upon her. "Go Quick!" cried the girl, and a motnent later Ella was in the street again. i "0 God! What shall I do? What shall do ? " she cried in despair. I Alone in the Golden City. Alone amidst tbe teeming thousands of gold-seekers. Here was 5131' seeking human love and sympathy, and findiat, none, save from an unfortunate girl placed bl position even worse than her -own. ; Into the busy streets she passed once more,wher: a babel of sounds filled the air, and above all th —thud----thud—boom—boom—of a big drum and tb° rattle of tambourines was heard. "The Salvatio* Army ! " ejaculated Ella in surprise. Yes, here were the followers of General Bootbk' as in far-off England, exhorting their hearers to see.r salvation. "Here, at any rate, I shall find help," thongli Ella. "These people will be kind to me." She waited until the service ended, then, as el? procession marched off, she followed in its viat`; Thrice was she accosted by impudent fellows Wm; sought to detain her, but she held on her way. "Come in, sister!" a kindly voice said AM' , motherly soul led her forward. That night and for many nights following. found rest rest in the Salvation Army shelter. - (To be continued. )4t

PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE.

II 50. Prosecutor turned ro rod and walked with him, talking about the weether. Prcsecutor askel him to go down the steps and he (witness) thought that be lived there and was going to lead him a cep. Witness did not drag him down the steps and never put his hands rear him. He had never been down the steps before: When they got to the bot• tom of the steps prostcutor wanted him to commit an indecent act and witness refused to do so Hope then gave him the butch of keys, purse, knife and 33 10d in money. The money consisted of a half-crown, is and tour pennies. He never put his hand in Hope's pocket nor did he act indecently or throw him oil the round. All but 33 101 of the 1.0 Od. pr tduced was Lis own menet?. Witness left the man as soon as he eave him the money and articles and went on his way home, meeting P.C. Howard. There was no occasion for him to rob anyone as he bad money of his own. His was down the steps about four minutes at the most. They did not struggle at all. By Superintendent Monaghan: He could not account for the state of Hope's clothing. When he left him he was all right. He intended to give the money and articles to P.C. Woods the next morning and he told the prosecu- tor bO. Constable Woods was stationed near his house. Mr. Browne then addresse 1 the Court. Fle said it was one of the strangest cases it had ever been his lot to appear in. In the first place Clarke was not the ordinary class of, prisoncr usually charged with committing a robber with violence. It was generally some corner- man, a well known man to the police who was charged with such an offence. Prisoner in this case was a most respectatle mao, had been in c-instent work, and Mr. Thompson, of the Mersey White Load Company, gave him an excellent chari- cter. Ora Friday he drew his wages, paid 123 for his board, 5s 3d arrears, and gave his father and mother 6s. There was an extraordinary feature of the case. Beth men maile a similar charge ; gaintt ea eh tithe:. Prisoner gave his evil !Ice very straightlerwarlly without reserve and truth- fully to a degree. On the ()tier hand, Mr. Hope, it was admitted by a witness for tiv prosecute!), was a drunken man, and it wa- for the Beech to weigh between them what actually did occur. What corroboration had they of the prosecutor's state ? Practically none, except that he had his hat dinged and his cluthing was covered with dirt. He suggeated that it would not he safe to commit the man and s-nd him for trial for robbery with violence en the evidence adduced beforo them. Mr. Jordan said they were troubled with persons committing nuisances down there. It was nonsense for the prosnutor to say that he was drageed down. He might have been a helpless kitten. He had only to raise the alarm and the people in the house would no dnibt have come to Ws assistat ci Be did not attempt to do se an;l it therefore pointed , that his tale was a lame one and that when he found he could not get in his own house he made up his mind to go to the Police Sretion. He did not get to the Police Station until 12 45 and if he had walked from Bank Quay Bridge he would have met a policeman but he did not seem to have done so. As regarded the prisoner not giving the money and articles to Constable Howard, Mr. Browne said that P C. Woods was looked upon as the lr cal policeman at Sankey Bridges,and it was reasonable to suppose that prisoner would have given them to him its the morning. When apprehended, he produced the keys, knife and eurse, and swore that the roan gave them to him together with 3s 101 in cash. lie (Mr. Browne), ventured to submit that it was an extra- ordinary case and one that should be amply corroborated before tkey came to the coneleeion that any j tarp would ever fled the man guilty of the set ious crime of robbery with violence. He did not need t 3 rob anyone, and it wail &mole a drunken freak on the part of the prosecutor which resulted in giving the money and articles away. The magistrates (Mesa's. J reirclough and S Birchen), committed the prisoner for trial to the Liverpool Assizes, bail being allowed.

The first rnee—ting- of thm newly-term,d Parochial Corn- mittee was held in the National Schools last Thursday evening. There were present Messrs Davenport,Whitley, Fairhurst, Mclntyre. Mason, Mounfield. Pemberton, Clarke, Farrington (nuisaace inspector), Swinton (sur- veyor), and G F Ashton (dark). ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN.

Mr. Whitley proposed th4t Mr: Davenport be re- elected chairman for the ensuing year. He had honour- ably carried out his duties during the past year and he had great pleasure in proposing him. Mr. Mclntyre secondAd, and said Mr. Davenport had served them well as a District Councillor: The motion was carried unanimously. Mr. Davenport then to•ik the chair and thanked the members for the renewal of their confidence.

div.head: VICE-CHAIHMAN
div.p: THE VICE-CHAIHMAN
Mr. G. H. Mason, was re-elocted vice.chairman on the motion of Mr. Fairhurst, secnnded by Mr Mclntyre.
COMMITTEES.

Messrs. Divenport, Pilling, ?arson, Pemberton,Clarke, Whitley and Mounfield were appointed as a building committee, and the lighting committee consisted ol Messrs. Mason, Pilling, Pearson, Pemberton, Mclntyre, Fairhurst and Whitley.

ELECTRIC LIGGITING FOR TER VILTAGE. The Clerk alluded to the motion ot Mr. Pemberton with reference to electric lighting in the village which was not discussed at the last meeting. Mr. Pemberton suggested that a committee should b appointed to consider the matter so that they might pro- tect themselves against anything which the corporation might do. Once the Corporation obtained powers they would have no redress. Mr. Mounfield thought Mr Pemberton had some scheme to bring forward. The Chairman thought if Mr. Pemberton was not pre. pared to bring a scheme forward it would be better to di far the matter. It was decided to defer the matter until the neat meeting. THE INSPECTOR AND SURVEYOR FORGET.

At the last meeting the Inspector and Surveyor were instructed to prepare a report on the naming of streets and numbering of houses. Mr. Farrington said he must confess he had forgotten all about it and the Surveyor informed him that he had also forgotten. He would report on the matter at the next meeting.

div.head: STREET MAKING
div.p: STREET MAKING

Mr. Mason asked -i-f—daitc-e-li=s-Creet and other streets were to be paved or macadamised ? The Clerk said they would be macadamised ? Mr. Mason said a property owner had consulted him on the matter as if the streets were paved he was going to sell his property to avoid the expense of paving. Tho Clerk said they were sure to be macadamised. This was all the business of public interest.

div.head: Trades Unionists' Church Parade.
div.p: Trades Unionists' Church Parade.

• • -- - - - Under the auspices of the Warrington Trades and Labour Council a Church parade should have taken place last Sunday aftarnooa. Owing to the wretched weather which prevailed the event was postponed. At a meeting of the Council held on Tuesday even- ing it was decided that the parade should be held to-morrow (Sunday), if the weather is favourable.

THE EXAMINER, FRI DAY, MAY 11 1900.
WARRINGTON CHAMBER OF
COMMERCE.
The L. and N.W. Railway Service.
Mr. C E Parker presided at a meeting of the Warring- ton Coainbta of Commerce held at Marlict Gate Chambers.

THE POSSIBILITIES OF THE CHAMBER. The SECRETARY (Ceuncillor Bsrinetc), read a report upon his attendance at tte annual meetiag of the secretaries of the Chambers of Commerce of the United Kingdom, on Tuesday, the 13q1 Maroh, at London. The chair was occupi(el by Mr. Elijah Helm, the secretary of the Manchester Chamber. Discussions, he said, were introduced by the Chairman on" Tri," Ideal Chamber," by Mr. Kenric B. Murray, the secretary of the London Chamber, on "Some Possible Developments of Cham- bers of Commerce Work." and by Mr. 1. Keens. jun , the secretary of the Luton Chamber and convener of the meeting. cii " The Work of a Ceamber of Commerce in the Smaller Provincial Towns." It was suggested amengst other thiegs, that " The Ideal Chamber," should include representatives of every manufacterine and whelesale business in its immediate neighbnurhood; that it should be sobsidivd by the Government ; stud that all commercial literature which is received, and which was of a permanently interesting character should be duly bound and tabulated. Luton, he learnt, was a typical instance of a pregreseive chamber. Under the active management of Mr. Keens its membership hasl increased, in four years from fifty to a hundred and forty ;it include, how- ever, like most of the chambers, a large number of retailers; was divided into sections ; and paid special attention to its sosial side, its annual functions inclusling a dinner, addressed, if possible, by some prominent public man, an excursion, and a cenversazione and dance. These elements no doubt did much to account for its Success, but, in every way, it WAS a striking illus- tration of the work which might be achieved by a chamber of commerce in a small provincial town. The Manchester Chamber had established a testing house for local goods, and the Lsndon Chamber was reeereed as a centre for all sorts of commercial information second only to the Imperial Institute or the Commercial Intellig- ence Department itself. Amongst other interesting facts, he learnt that Swansea basted two lady members ; and it was once ag.in impressed upon him that the scope of Chambers of Commerce was practically unlimited; that, apart altogether ficim their collective ielluence, they could be (14 enormous service to their own localities ;And that, in Warrinetort, their uFefulness is only limited by the apathy of those to whom they had a right to look for active and intelligent support. He also attended the fortieth annual meting of the Asseciated Chambers, on the 13th, 14 h, and 15th March. The discussions were, as usual, extremely interesieg, and more than forty motion's had been pieced on the official programme. THE LONDON AND NORTH-WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY'S

Tile SECRETARY read the following correspondence be- tween the Chamber and the London and North-Western Railway Company, and reported that, as a result of a conference between the Chamber, the Town Council,and the C oteptny, other concessions had beera promised, and that the Company had met their representatives in a very friendly spirit. " Market Gate Chambera. Warrington, January B'h, 1900. I) ,ar Sir,—My Council desire me to call attention to the fact that there is not any commueication between London and Warrington by the London and North- Western Railway after 530 p.m., nor ar y communica- tion between Werrington and the North front 8 p.m. to 6 a.m., ner any connection at Crewe with the Shrews- bury and South Wales traffic latrr than the train which reaches Warrington at 937 p.m., nor any c emmuni!et- the between North Wales and Warrington after 5 5., from Rhyl, and that the 3.20 train from Warrington te London and the train connecting with the London mail from Liverpool to Crewe at about 10.45 have each been ttken off. These circumstances constitute a serious public inconvenience, and myCounail are of opinion that Warrington is not treated by your Company with the consideration to which it is entitled as a great and rapidly-increasing industrial centre. They trust that you will be able to see yreir way to modify the arrange merits comp'ained of,and will be glad to hear your views in the matter in due course.—Faithfully yours, ARTHUR geureerr, hon. secretary." " London and North-Western Railway,Euston Station London, N.W , April 20. h, 1900. Dear Sir.—ln reply to your letters of January Bth and Arril 11th addresied to the secretary of the company. I have ta inform you that we cannot see our way to again stop the 10 p.m. express from Easton at Warrington,but during July and eug.ust pisseneers from Warringtoa can travel by the 955 p.n.. train and joie at Wigan,the 11 10 p.m. express which will be run to Carlisle to connect with the 7.45 p.m. tourist express from Euston to the Highland line (which will run from July 20:h to the end of August), the 8 p no. express from Euston to Oban,Perth,A.herdeen an i beyond, ad the 8 10 p.m. from Eaten to St anraer. With regard to the service from North Wales during the summer months, a train will leave Bangor at about 6 25 p.m..Llendudno, 6 50 peneand Rhcl at 7 45 p.m., and reaching Warrington at about 9.15 p.m., whisk will, I have re) doubt, meet the wishes of your Council. I am sorry we cannot see our way to again stop the 9 5 a.m. express; from Perth at Warrington, but woold point out that when this step was withdrawn another service was given leaving Warring,on at 25 p.m, and reaching Euston at 625 p m. During the sumener.also, the even- jac service.eow leaving Warrington at 5 20 p.m. and ar- riving in Elston at 10 25 p.m. will be much impreved by leaving Warrington at 5 p.m. and arriving in London a' 930 p.m. As regards the latter part of your letter of the Bea January. there see me to be some misapprehen- sion, as the 10 45 p.m. from Liverpool to Stockport still cennects at Warrington with the up mail due to vach Eaut on at 350 a.m.—Yours le ally, R. Turnbull." PROPOSED REFORM IN PARLIAMENTARY ELECTIONS. It ve,s decided, on the suggestion of the Liverpool Chamber, to memorialize the Government in • favour of holding all B orouge elections on one day and all county elections within a week.

div.head: MOTHER SEIGEL IN INFLUENZA
div.p: MOTHER SEIGEL IN INFLUENZA

He hAted to give up, Mr. Bootes did, but he had to. There was only one road for him to travel by. .T...st when business was so pushing at the Stores, too !—bat was the unluckiest part of it, so he thought.

T. ado was booming, and the manager was far from wanting to be hid on his back. Let the fellows who have plenty of time on their hacds—lct thens go into dry dock, but not a man that begrudges the very,hours spent in

slew. Sa our friend tried to ignore his feelings ; he tried, as the children ray to" make believe " nothing ailed him. "Only a bit of a cold," he argued ; "I shall be all right in A day or two; can't afford to be laid on the shelf n aw."

Strong talk, hopeful talk ; yet all the same Mr. Arthur J. Bootes, of Wyscotnbo Villa, Orpington. Bent, mana- ger of Goodwin's Grocery Storm in that town, was obliged to drop everything and take to his bed with a vicious attack of influenza.

In a letter dated January 10. 1900,Mr. Bootes says r— " I was in bed for a fortnight, completely prostrated. For over three days I was delirious, I ached from heael to foot ; there didn't seem to be a spot in my body without its own individual pain. "But it is not necessary for me to describe influenza, as most pe via in England know what it is like,froin ex_ perience or observation. " I ought to mention that for years before this I had been subject to a pain in the left side, and in this par- ticular place the influenza appeared to grip me hardest ; and it left me with pleurisy in that side. At times the pain was so sharp i could not stand upright ;it steined to draw my side right in, and took away my breath. I took many things to ease this pain without any permanent relief. But I am getting ahead of my story. " Of the pain in the side I was completely cured by a.,:plying a Mother Seigel's Soothing Plaster, and the same remedy cured the pains caused by the influenza. " Now that infleenza is again prevalent I recommend threkl plasters as an outward application, and Mother Seigel's Syrup to drive the disease out of the bloed. By th use of the two any attack of influenza may be cured —of that I am persuaded." Better still to use Mother Seigel's Syrup daily in smal, doses during the continuance of the influenza epidemic, It will maintain the body in high health and prevent an attack.
Had Mr. Bootes done this he would not have lost several weeks' time from business.

div.head: 1 WARRINGTON BAND OF HOPE UNION. Sale of Work.
div.p: 1 WARRINGTON BAND OF HOPE UNION. Sale of Work.

OPENING BY THE MAYOR & MAYORESS. Since its inauguration the Warrington and Ustrict Band of,Hope U,d3n has accomplished 8.91113 ueeful work, hilt unfor unately it has got into debt. The deficit of £55 has accumulated atid this fPedied to threaten the tut ure usefulness and activity of the Union. A sale of work was decided upon as a means of removing the debt and since that decision was arrivei at a number of hand of hope friends— have b-en busily engaged in making articles for tbe sale. The result was seen on the stallm at the sale of work which was opened in the Masonic Hall on Wednesday afternoon. There were four stalls, and they contained a large number of useful and fancy

aTiVele;:--The following ladies were in charge : No 1 Stall : Mrs J Yong,e, Misses F Baswick,Pearson, Critchley, and Dreyer No. 2 Stall: Mrs Mounfield. Mrs Shaw, Miss Annie lienworthy, Miss C Birch,and Mrs Shaw. No. 3 S all : Mr. Braystiaw, Mrs Elea, Miss Morin- field, and Miss Brsmhall. No. 4 Stall : Miss C Dale, Mrs Colley, Mrs O'Brien, Mss Carter and MiS3 Siddail. In addition there was a refreshment stall in charge of the following ladies :—Miss Shaw GrPe3, Mrs Hatohin, Mrs Hallow-3s, Miss elailowes, Miss Prince, Miss Moun

fitild, Miss Smith, and Miss Strange. Tne room wa3 well filled at the opening ceremony. Amongst thcse present were the lAyer and Mayumss (Aldermen and Mrs Roberts), Mr R A Ntylot (presinent of the Union), Revs F E Po sell, J Yong" 141 T Red, J F Matthews, C Finch, J r Schofield, Messrs Win. Roberts, Thuna4s Dile, T Ashley, F Morrell, and E Lloyd Jones

(secretary): Mr. R. A. Neeecirs conducted the proceedings, which opened with the singing of a hymn specially composed for the oceasion by the Rev. J F Matthews, of Latch- ford. Toe Rev. F E Powell then offered prayer. Mr. E LLOYD-JONE4 presented a sta.ternent explaining the object of the sale, which he stated was to clear off ae adverse balance in connection with the Band of HOpo Union. The organisation had only been in existence 16 months, but during that time a considerable amount of work had been done whi ih had estailed expense. Too choir, for instance, which had rendered excellsnt service and which they hoped would do more is the future, had cost a good deal, especially in the purchase of music They had entered the competitive examinations for Lan- cashire and Cheshire during the year, and the children in connection with their Bands of Hope in VVarrineton and 4 strict came out of them very creditably. (Hoar, hear.) They had also half-a-dozen rallies, which were very suc- cessful, not only from the attendance standpoint, but also frem a financial point of v;ees, wHa perhaps one exception. The rallies in the open air were very sueesseful, and at one rally alone they wad an attendasice of 2,500, and a large number of pledges were taken. This was very eecouraging, but they were unable to make any charge at the °pee air rallies and coaseqaently the expenses fell on the Union. At the present time the adverse balance amounted to £55. The room in which the choir met cost teem a considerable sum. The Union had been handicapped in reisine sub, scriptions owing to other societies claiming the support of the temperance people of Warrington. There were 23 societies affiliated with the union, representing all denominations in the town,but only a few had been able to give assistance at that sale of work. The following societies bad assisted • British Women's Tern- nerance Association. Stockton Heath and Hill Cliffe United Band of Hope, Wycliffe, Bank Quay Mission, Cairo-street, Bold-street, Friars'-Green, St. James', Pad. gate Wesleyan. fhe other s3ciaties had failed to do so in consequence of being engaged on sales of work in con- nection with their own denominations. In conclusion be desired to thank all who had assisted for the excellert results of their work, (Ape 'awe ) Mr. R. A. NLYLIR stated that the Band of Hope Union had done a very useful work in the town and neighbour- hood and there was no doubt whatever that there was a great week to be done. Mere was every necessity for renewed and conttnued exertions. They perhaps did not apply themselves with the sa me determination and enthusiasm whick characterised the efforts of the temperance peonies of that town a few years azo. They eould not get away from the fact that a great many were addicted to habits of intemperance. Through mt the British Isles there was a great deal of drunkenness in spite of all the efforts which the various temper- ance organisations bad put forth. Judging by the, Board of Trade returns he did not think that temperance people could congratulate themselves upm. having achieved very much. The revenue from the consumption of intoxicante was on the increase, and therefore there must be more drinking. It might be argued that the drink was distributed among a greater number of inhabitants and that there was not a larger proportion of drunkards, but when they saw a drink bill such as was presented by the Board of Trade, no really sensible patriotic man could arrive at any other conclusion than that there was still too much drinking of intoxicants for the good of the community. (Heal, hear.) He did not know what their Band of Hope Union proposed to do in the future but there was a vast field of usefulness. He was glad to see present that day representatives of nearly all the churches and chape's in the town. Temperance was a subject on which they could sink all differences of opinion and unite together for the good of common humanity. (Applause.) The MAYOR said he was very glad indeed to nave as opportunity of showieg by his presence there that afternoon, his intense sympathy with the work of the Band of Hope Union in Warrington. (Hear, hear.) Both he and his wife had been life long abs'ainers and both Of them had baen members of bands of hope in this town. If they did not take that active part in the work they once did, it was not from any want of earnest and intense sympathy with the movement, but because other duties now took up so much of their time teat it was impossible for them te take the same active interest in band of hope work. When they had an opportunity they were only ton pleased to show their sympathy in a practical way. Whilst he agreed with the remarks of the chairman as to the need of increased effert he did not quite agree with the slightly pessimistic view which the cireirman took of the temperance party to-day. It was quite true that their drink bill was bigger than ever, but they must remember that our prosperity at the present time was ereater than over and that our population wa

ids' greater. He was bound to say ^that speatrineo generally the lives of the people of this country had shown a marked and distinct improvement in regard to drink during the last fifteen years, largely the result, he thought, of the efforts of band of hope societies. It was also an undoubted fact that in spite of the heavy drink bill they had a greater number of pledged abstainere whose habit of life and example were such that ia the long run their influence must be of immense good upon the people of this country. Temperance work had taken a move forward in consequence of the repert of the Cone_ 'pinion which recently set under the presidency of Lord Peel. The remarkable thing about the Commission was not that two reports were presented differing on cert sin points, but that there were so many points on which the Commission were agreed. (Hear, hear.) He v.ould be satisfied if Isgislation upon the points on which the commission were absolutely agreed could be put illiso operation. He Was certain that the result would be for the immenqe improvement of t'ae condition of the people of the country. They welcomed legi,lation in regard to the proteetion or children. (Hear, heir.) The report of the Commission on this subjert,t he amount of pubic feeling favourable to it, and the result of the division in the House of Lords on toe previous night in respect to it, all testified that the pawl of the country were practically uneesimous in their demand that young children up to 16 years of age should be protected by the legieiature from the temptation which the friiquent attendance at public-houses was likely to lead them into. Then again, when they compared their positions as temperance workers with the po:ition of those who championed their cause fifty years ago they had every reason to take couraee and thank God and be hopeful for the future: (Hear, hear.) He believe l the band of hope was not only the most useful but the most impor taut branch of temperance work. They all knew haw utterly hopeless it was to expect men and women to re- form whose habits of intemperance had become fixed. He did not nerd to illustrate this but it must be within the recolleetion of everyone present how very seldom it was that when persons got over 40 years of age anything in the shape of reform in the habit of taking drink, was possible. He wee not going to enter into the question, but except by the grace of God very few glen reformed after they reached that age. But if the children were trained in the habits of total abstinence and were con- firmed in those hebits by their aesociatien with bands of hope and kindred societies and by their experience and knowledge of the truths which were talight them, they remained steadfast to temperance principles, and as the result they had a vast number of total abstainers of both eexes. He wished every success to the band of hope union because he thought a combination of all the bands of hope was bound by its moral effect to make a con- siderable amount of progress which the isolated efferte of the eocietiee was practically enabled to do. (Ap plause.) The MAYORESS in declaring the sale of work open said she very heartily wished it success. She hoped they would clear the stalls and leave behind them a very substantial balance to carry on the work for another year. (Applause.) Mr. R. A. NAYLOR in proposing a vote of thanks to the Mayor and Mayoress, expressed the wish that all the Mayors and Mayoresses in the country were tctal abstainers. Mr. Tereates DATA'. chairman of the executive creel-

Imittee, seconded the vote of thanks and referred to the encouragiog remarks which had fallen from the lips et the Mayor and Mayoress. Those who laboured in band 3 f hope work needed encouragment for there were many who were re .:17 to discoorage them. The pr,poaition was unanimously carried. Toe MAYOR acknowledged the cordial appreciation of the preseuce of his wife and himself. The I' v. J. YoNon proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. R. A. Naylor, for presiding, and remarked that every- thing counezmeol with tomperance appealed to Mr. Naylor's heart and was sure to command his presence and support. (Hear, hear.) Mr. WILLIAM Roman seconded the vote of thanks aed stated teat the Temperance Federation thoroughly desired that the work of the band of hope union might be thoroughly successful. It was the intentioa of the Temperance 'Federation to vo`e a sum of money towards the object of the sale of work. The vote was unanimously carried, and Mr. NAYLOR having acknowledged the complimeot, the bale commenced. Entertainments were provided in the evening. The takings for the day amounted to £3O: The sale WAR again opeeed on Thurrday but there was no formal ceremony.

div.head: FATALITY TO A BOY.
div.p: FATALITY TO A BOY.
A Need for Public Playgrounds.

The daneers of swinging behind lorries, carts, and other vehicles, a practice pretty general amongst tip boys of Warrington,on Thursday afternoon last resulted in the loss of a life. Between four and five o'clock a carter employed by Mr. Sudlow, contractor, Church- street, was coming down Scheol-brow, into Manchester- road, when a little boy, Thomas Ball, aged 5, the son of William end Mary Ball, 22, Manchestereroad,caught hold behind and ',need to swing his feet upon the axle tree so as to enjoy a ride in that dangerous position. His legs, however proved too short and they got entangled in the spokes of the wheel with the result that the boy was wound up and got his skull fractured between the wheel and axle —On Friday Mr F A Joces,deputy rorone:,held an inquest on the body at the Warrington Police Court —Marc Ball, the deceased's mother, gave evidence of identificatien, adding that her son came home from school aneut ten minutes past four. About twenty minutes later he went out into the street to play. A piffle later she nad occasion to go to the front daor from whence she saw a trawd congregated lower down the street. Upon inquiry she found her bty had been injured. Dr. McCarthy was called in and stated that the child was suffering from a fracture of the base of the skull. A few hours later he died.—W !Ham Bibby, a neighbour's five year old andel, , described to the Coroner how the accident occurred. which was in the manner described above.—Feaek Done, a young man, who happened tao he in the s-reet, said the first intimation of anything wrong that ho got was hearing the screams of the boy Bad. He ooked round anal saw tee little fellow being drawn tinder the tow* of the lorry. He called out to the driver and he stopped iestantty.—Paul Hankinson, the driver, stated when coming down School Brow he noticed two children in the street and that was all. He passed them hut did not knov one of them hid gone to swing beoind. Neither did anyone call out "Whip Behind I" He heard the child scream and was stopped by the last witnesi.— In summing up tha Coroner said it was clearly a death caused accidentally.—The jury concurred. The Foreman (Mr G J Craik) alluded to the want of playing ground accommodation,and operalspaces for the Warrington children to play in. He was of opinion there shoul I be one for each Ward, The Coroner : Well. Novr's your time. Solto it at the next election of the Corporation. A. Juror ; Yes. We will get the promises all right. chat is all. (Laughter). Mr Craik : I believe there are no bye-laws for pre- venting children running after carts, etc. 'the Coroner: A bye-law doesn't prevent it. It only provides a penalty for the breach of it. The Foreman : But the police have no power to interfere with the children in Warrington. The Coroner : If I SAW anything of the kind I should try to prevent it. Of course I would have no leen right, but there wsuld be a strong moral right for inter ference. However he would communicate with the corp oration if they required, or let it go as an exrression fro the Press. A jurior : It is my opinion that children would go after carts even if there were plenty of play grounds.
