Ohmy's Circus. Patrons of this popular place of amusement have been admirably catered for during the pa,t week. A. first-rite programme has been submitted, the principal item being the entertainment by the Steens, the well-known American mvstifyers. These artistes who claim to be the originators of silent transmission, give a really surprising exhibition of what is terrned"Second sight sorcery" The Misses Maud and Gracie Steen act as double mediums and answer questions put by the members of the audience as to the whereabouts of their rela- tions, their age, date of birth, Christian names etc. Figures and names are written on b'ackboards be gentlemen selecte I from the audience, and to the astonishment of the onlookers, the Misses Steen, who are blindfolded add up the figures with accuracy and name any letters or figures pointed to. The most mysterious part of the whole performance, however, is the " Egyptian Sarcophagus " illusion. Two apparently strong trunks with brass rcounts imad corner pieces are placed in the ring. Professor Steen then intro- duces two young ladies to the audience. One or the ladies is placed in a sack which is securely tied by a member of a committee selected from the audience The committee having examined the boxer, the lady is then placed in the smallest one which is doubly locked and cer:s tied round it. This b,x is then lifrAed into the largeene which is also doubly locked and secured. A. screen is then placed rounn the boxes and the second young lady stands behind it. The word" Go "is given, and in a few seconds, the young lady who had ' been locked in the boxes emerges aril leaves the ring. The boxes are then unlocked and inside the sack to the surprise of all the second young lady is found.—Another pleasing feature of the evening's entertainment is the graceful performance of Miss Dahlia, who goes through some difficult feats on the high trapeze. The Tarras give aju gling exhi- bition with great dexterity, and little Toney, the champion boy rider, appears in a jockey act. Of the other " turns " perhaps the most popular is that provided by Miss Myer's troupe ef dogs which display unusual sagacity. The clowns Gartland, Walker and Hoppet,enliven the entertainment with their witticisms and little Lilly. the child rider, wins hearty plaudits. use Watson is successful as an equestrienne. This afternoon a day perform- ance will take place.

FATALITY AT THE HELSBY CABLE WORKS. A Young Man Suffocated in a Gutta- Percha Tank. At the Helsby Club and Institute, on Monday rnorning Mr. J. C. Bate, coreeer, held an inquest upon the body of William Martin Little, a gutta-petcha worker, who lest his hfe on Friday morning last whilit following his employment at the Helsby Telegraphic Manufacturing Conspane's Wee k 4.—Mr. Erant, assistant factories in- spector, Liverpool, was present ;as also was Mr. James Feeler (one of the Compeey's Directors) ; and the police were represented hy Serge.nt Clays (Frodsham). William Joseph Little, said he Yves the father of the deceased and resided at B,edbury, Stockport, near Man- chester. His son was 22 years of age and a gutta-percha worker in the employ of the Telegraphic Manufacturing Company at Relsby. Only as late as Easter-Tuesday bis son had told him he liked both his work and his lodgings and was very comfortable. lisbert Baxter, lateurer, in the employ of the Tele- graphic Manufacturing Company, on the 4th of May, was engaged with another man named William Pope in carrying eutta-nercha to and from the " Golf bell shed." thout 11 o'clock Pope ask el him to see whether Little had t :ken all tee gutta-percha out of the tank. He did so and was astonished to see Little lying at the bottom, with Ilia hid against the end. He got into the tank and lifted Lister's ouleand then called for Haelehurst, tee foreman. Deceased was carried outside and witness immediately ran for Mr. Barlow, the head of the am- bulance. Witnecs did not see any sign of life hut he did not think Little was dead. He h d not worked in the reek himself and had no experience of the effects of the fumes. WilliensJehn Hszlehurst, foreman of the gutta-percha purifying departmeet, said he had 15 years' experionce of the work. William Martin Little was one of the men engaged ender him. The process of purifying the gutta-percha was one for tee abstraction of the resin. Strips of the raw gutta-percha were put into tanks, and covered with spi-its of p-troleum. This in turn was covered over and left for 24 hnirs. The liquid was then drawn off and distilled to prevent waste, and the tanks were again filled with fresh spirits. The process was repeated for one or two days, after which the cover was removed from the tack and the process of discharging I carried out by hand.—The Coroner : If the cover is ' only removed when you are going to discharge there will be a consieerable escape of vapour P—Witness : Yes—Are any measures taken to ventilate the room be- fore the discharging goes on ?—lt has always bee; my rule, sir, to leave the door open. But it being a windy day deceased had evidently shut it to prevent the eutter-pereha sheets from being blown ahnut.—Did you give him any instructions about that P—Yes sir.—Continuing, Witness said deceased was the only man workine under him at that jots. It was almest a daily occurrence for witness to be affected by the fumes, which seed upon one sending them to sleep. The large tank (No. 6) which the deceased was engaged in emptying held three rows of gutta-percha strips. The two first rows could be em ,tied from the enfolds., but the bottom row could only be emptied by going iato the tank. He left the decease lat 10.20 a.m. about to cernmenc s discharging, and at 11 o'clock he came hank and looking into the room found that de-eased had discharged as he thought at the time, the whole of the contents of the tank. He found out subse- quently, however, that there were about half-a-dozen strips left in the tan'e, and suggested that probably the deceased was becoming affected by the famesand think- ing he could have discharzed all before becoming over- came had tried to do so with fatal results. In all his experience witness had only bad one troublesome case before. Mr. James Taylor, 010 of the direntors of the Tele- graphic alanufacturine Company. submitted plans of the iseileines showing the system of ventilation to be a most elaborate one. Mr. Taylor said nothing further I awe be done in the way of ventilation except with mechanical aid—such as fani.pri. accnunt,however,of the danger of tirineine any heaVnear the building because of the infleminability of tett fumes it was not thought advisab'e to do so. It was of course easy enough to be wise after the event and be had already given instruc- tions that two men should always be present for the future at the discharging of the large tanks. The door he had himself ordered to be always left open when anyone was inside, so that in c iso of fire there would he means of escape. There was plenty of ventilation with- out taking the door into cnnsideratlon. Dr Brient, Helsbe, said he was called in about 11 o'c'ock on tee 4 hof May and found the deceased dead at the Cable Works. He had visited the room and re- mained in the funaes sufficiently long to be affected by them. In his opinion the deceased had been first intoxi- catei by the fumes, and then fall-en down to the tra"fom of the tank and been gradually suffocated. He has] no nrevayas experience of such a case. Mr. Brant seid from the evidence of the man who act, d as foreman it was pre ti' clear how the man had come to his death. Ms th aught that certain further pre- cautions ought to be taken to prevent a recurrence of such a fatality'. The Coroner had suggested to him,and he quite agreed with it, that it was vice necessary for two men to be in the room sahilst the work was going on, and he WAS of epinion there should be a suitable inter- val from the time the cover of the tank was removed to when the work of discharging was commenced. Tres question of ventilation was already covered by the Fac- tory Acts. He might say tban the question of working in petroleum of any kind had been before his department for sometime past, and as a result certain recommenda- tions were before the Home Office Legislation Com- mittee, but to a great extent he was able to say that they were mostly already in vogue at the Telegraphic Manufacturing Company's Works. The Coroner, in summing up, said it was quite within the province of a jury in a case of that kind to make any recommendation thee thought fit. Mr. Taylor had told them that for the future he had given orders that one man should no longer work alone in the room. That had occurred to him as a solution from the start, for when two men were present and anything happened there would be one to help the other out. In his opinion the deneased owed his death to purely accidental causes. and he did not think any blame could be attached to anyone. The jury came to the conclusion, after quarter of an hour's deliberarion, that the man died from "accidental causes" brought anoiat in the manner described by the medical evidence.—They were also of opinion that means should be provided for emptying the largo tanks without necessitating a man going into them, and sugeested that shallower tanks should be used. Then, even if a , man was overcfrme, he would fall to the floor and being I out of reach of the fumes which would naturally rise, there would be less risk. The Coroner said possibly Mr. Taylor, who was pre- sent, would note the recommendatioa. Mr. Taylor said the recommendation would receive attention. Tbe Company had for some time been con- sidering the erection of a cradle pulley arrangement for loading and discharging the tanks which would obviate the need of entering the tanks, and it would be carried out very shortly.

div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
CRICKET.

Warrington almost—but not quite, EucceeVd in gain- ing a vict3ry over Cheadle Hulste on the Arpley Ground on Saturday. The game was a most interesting one. Batting first Warrington ran up the respectable total of 172 for seven wickets. Cheadle wi.re then sent in to bat and just succeeded in saving the match their score reach- ing 91 for the loss of eight wickets. The match was noticeable for the brilliant batting of Thewlis and Dr. Smith, the former kaneking no 64 and Dr. Smith 67 not out. Time alone prevents-I Warrington from securing a victory which they thoroughly deserved.

Thawlis and Silcock tatted first,the former scoring the first sixteen runs when he lost the company of Si(cock. who failed to time a fast one from Teather. J Callon came next, and opened his account well by placing Tether square f.-ir four. Runs came freely until at 38 a time stroke by the amateur placed one in the hands of Williams at mid-off. E. Connor came next, and another useful stand was mad, the majority of the runs coming from tiae professioaat's bat. A beautiful late cut by Thewlis raised the score to fifty, as a result of as many minutes' play, and Cadman was called upon to relieve TeathAr, and in his third over bowled Connor. Dr. Smith, who appeared in the horns team for the first time this season, joined Tnewlis, and a fine stand was now witnessed. The bowling was collared, each bats- man hitting all round the wicket.

Mason was tried in place of Cadman, but Thewlis treated him in an unceremonious manner, whilst 'Feather was called upon again only to be despatched to the boundary by Dr. Smith, this drive causing the cen- tury to be hoisted amid cheers. Thewlis completed his fifty a few minutes later,and though Redfern resumed at the scoring box tad the batsmen were now thoroughly pet, whilst the fielding at times became very loose. Williams was tried for an over, and was then promptly replaced by Teather, a separation not being effected until the aggregate had reached 143, when Dwayne was caught at cover point for a finely hit 64 made without a. blemish. His innings includei nine boundary strokes. G Clarke joined Dr. Smith,but the last named chiefly occu- pied the attention of the scorers, and this partnership yielded 21. runs when Clarke W 39 bowled for five. Thompson returned the first ball ha received, and the total was taken to 172 when R Conner was run out and the closure was applied, Dr. Smith having spade 67 without giving the !semblance of a chance, his innings including nine boundary strokes.

Cheadle Hulme commenc ei their inningsat five o'clock with the brothers A E and C H Taylor, the bowling be- ing shared by Thewlis and Or Smith. Runs came freely from the amateur and at 30, 3 W Bibby relieved him The new bowler immediatety met with success,disposing of A E Taylor with a fine ball. A useful stand was made by Cadman and C H Taylor, but runs only came slowly, the bowling being very fine. Cadman calved the half- century to be hoistei with a fine drive off Bibby, but seven rues later The is sent the amateur back for a patiently played 28. From this period Thewlis was well-nigh unplayable, and wickets fell in quick succes- sion. Cadman was bowled at 44, and at the same total C)nnor relieved his captain, the fast bowler shattering Williams' middle stump in his second over. Teather was finely caught at mid-on, whilst Thewlis also sent back Rome witheat scoring. Mason added five when Thewlis bowled him, the professional in the following over also getting past Redfern's defence, rhewlis in the last six avers having taken six wickets at a cost of six runs. G E Haworth and C Rome adopted • purely defensive tac- tics, and although W H Podia:tore and J W Bibby were tried in the last few minutes, the batsmen maietained their wicket intact, the score reaching 91 for the loss of eight batsmen.

div.head: SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A WARRINGTON BOY.
div.p: SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A WARRINGTON BOY.

_ The Result of a Fight. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, onSaturday before Messrs. T Birchall (in the chair) and R T Fair- dough, Fred Lencock, a hot-, residing at 37. Scotland- road, was charged with caugiug grievous bodily harm to a boy named Alfred &caetr, 37, Scotland-road, by striking him en the head with a stone in Bewsey-street at 10.15 en Friday night. Superintendent Monaghan, in applying for a remand until Wednesday.briefly stated the facts of the case inin which it appeared that the prisoner, Beckett and other boys wont to the circus and took part in 3 riding corn- petition.When they came out they Lad some dispute and prisoner's brother and Beckett quarrelled and fought. Prisoner took his brothres part arid he and Beckett also fought with the result that prisoner threw a stone at Beckett which struck him on the forehead, fracturing his skull. Beckett was taken to the Infirmary where be was detained as an inpatient and his condition was rattler serious. The remand was granted. Lencoek was again brought 13fore the magistrates on Wednesday. Superintendent Monaghan again narrated the facts af Ithe case and added that Beckett was progroasing favour- ably but was not yet nut of danger. He asked for a further remand for a week. Prisoner was remanded accordingly.

is public affairs nothing i 5 Want of Nerve, more likely to lead to disass ter and confusion than want of:nerve. It incapao" itates statesmen from doing the right thing et the right moment, and it leads to hesitation wile* promptneas is essential. Weak actions lead on to lack of confidence, and then strong Governmentsr come tumbling down before public disapproval' The present state of affairs, in the country and °L4 of it, calls for nerve of uncommon quality. Is it being displayed in high places at the present moment? In the conduct of the war in the field there have been delays, irritating to the public mind, and injurious to an early attainment of the end we seek, entirely due to the want of nerve e7hibited at home. It may not be easy to afaS responsibility to any one individual, but Tre know what has been lacking, and it is unnecesearY to repeat old facts and familiar criticisms. Eel" dences of the same tenuity of purpose have been seen in the military contracts inquiry. At first it seemed as if some persons were being shielded, and then there were prospects of a criminal prosecution. The prosecution was not pressed, and a committee of inquiry was granted insteso. But in the composition of that committee ecraa persons were omitted who clearly ought to have had seats upon it. No sooner had the committee got to work than an application was made—not in the interests of the army and the discovery of the truth, but for the protection of the very person; whose doings were to be investigated. A certain letter was declared to be a breach of the privilege; of the House of Commons. Ministers voted that such was the fact, and then lost nerve. The irrita- tion this his caused cannot be understood by the mere trivial observer. Followers want leading, and there are times when they look for it in vain. Government by strong men, with a docile majority, cug,ht not to subject the country to these unpleasant incidents. It always enjoYS firmness, sound policy, and resolute actioo• When these qualities are absent it asks whither events are tending; and it receives:l no answer. The appointment of a severe critic of the Adtninistration to be Postmaster; General was another instance of want 0- nerve, and the selection of a candid critic an Solicitor-General is another. Of what are Minister. afraid? That is what we all want to know. Th° Licensing Commission was appointed to lay the 1 basis of further reforms in an impartial and cool" prehensive spirit. It has done so, and el° Government is as nerveus and queer over legielir tion on the basis laid down as if it were asked t° commit political suicide. The question of Wes; sive ritual and Catholic practices in the Church he been handled in the same timid way. We were protaised legislation against aliens, and nothing more has been heard about the !natter. There wAs talk about revising the number of represent 6; tives from ha I incl. There is a demand for subniaill beats. A committee of inquiry into the manage: ment of the War Office has been promised, nothing has been done. Everywhere we detect - I lack of nerve, not due to the overshadowing ill' fluence of the war, but to some mental defects in the Administration itself. It is clearly time the country began to review these signs and Wild toms, in preparation for a great decision.

But the money of Monarchical parties can be spent in inventing 'levy cries and prejudices, and in clothing the bare bones of a repulsive spectre with the fine clothes °I a deceptive show. The Republicans are more national than the Nationalists, because they desire to retain popular government, in the interests of ttio whole country, instead of twisting national tallaire to suit the claims of Royal Families, and to 4eeP down the rule of the people to elevate the rule of the priests. There is no National:st who Can command attention and enthusiasm, who can Ptc)rniae attractive politics,who can hope to recover the loss provinces and restore France to herself Init. a military victor, a leading Power in the des- jainieB ef European countries. Mobs must have 'Qls, and M. Dorculede is not an idol—he is only Sign-post. Mobs must be animated by some idea °I gain, some enthusiasm of humanity. div.head: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
div.p: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
A Provincial Letter.

English farmers have no need of an outbreak of cattle-plague just now, to worry them, but the arrival in the Thames the other day of heavy con- signments bearing the unmistakable taint of foot- and-mouth disease, has certainly had the effect of causing much anxiety in the matter. It was known when these vessels landed that on one of them con- siderably more than two hundred animals had died from the disease on the voyage, and that on anotete• two hundred and eighty-three bullocks and tour hundred and fifty-two elseep had bean lost from the same cause. It is felt that the alertness of the Board of Agriculture officials may be sufficient to prevent the development of any evil effects of such a state of things, but, at the same time, the danger arising therefrom is not merely imaginary. It in- variably happens that foot-and-mouth disease can be traced to imported cattle, and it is for the Board of Agriculture to insist that at least these vessels shall be thoroughly disinfected before there is any traffic between them and the cattle-lairs at Dept- ford, and particularly to enforce the most stringent measures against the communication of the disease by animals after they have been landed. One of the things they de differently in France, not to say " manage better," has reterence to the way in which they treat wild riders of the auto-car. At Long Ashton Petty Sessions on Saturday, gentleman was fined twenty shillings and costs for furiously driving a motor car; while on the previous day fifty automebilists in Paris were each fined ten f ranc% and had to undergo one day's imprisonment as well, for a similar offence. The pecuniary ad- vantage to the court would seem to favour the English ruling,but probably the French is the most effectual.Anyhow,there are more than a few persons in this country who would like to see a day's im- prisonment added to the usual fine in the case of many of the sons of Nimshi on wheels brought be- fore local magistrates for riding furiously. The question of Old Aga Pensions has now had the serious attention of many Friendly -ocieties for years ; repeeted efforts have been made to keep the matter well in view, and numerous schemes have been proposed. The Labour illlectoral Association is at the present moment dealing with the proposal that a "Free State Pension" shall be the right of every man and woman over sixty-five years of age. The method of allowing such pensions was pro- pounded by Mr. Charles 139oth,and it is being advo- cated by the National Committee of Organised Labour, the different branches of which are about to hold meetings for the purpose of keepiog the general question before the public. Reference was made to the subject at the annual conference of the West Midland Poor-law Guardians on Friday, when the Chairman, Mr. S. Gateley, said tn at in his opinion no one should be entitled as a right to a Pension who could not show that he had made some p-ovision for his old age by his ()In efforts. The Cenference did not pass any resolution on the matter, but judging from the way in which the Chairman's statement was received, it seemed to embody the views of Poor-law Guardians of the West Midlands. It is perhaps not unnatural that many persons ehould at one time have wondered whether, when he was promoted to the Archbishopric of Canter- bury, Dr. Temple would remain loyal to his temper- ance principles. His name has been so often and eo prominently before the public of late in connec- tion with one scheme or another of temperance work and reform, that there is little need to answer the question now, except in the way of referring questioners to his numerous speeches on the sub- ject. The other day, his Grace, speaking at a meet- ing of the Natienal Temperance League, referred ie a way and with an effect which scarcely any other sinole individual could be expected to speak, of the change which has come over medical opinion on the suhi-ct. In the present day. as Dr. Temple pointed out, doctors are more open to conviction than for- merly, and evince a greeter desire to get at the truth in regard to this important question. Once upon a time, the advice to patients was in large part conventional, and offered because it was thought it would be welcome to the one who sought advice. There is not nearly so much of this now. His Grace's suegestion that children in the elementary schools should be taught the evils of the abuse of alcoholic beverages, is net new ; but the speeches cannot fail to be helpful to the movement which he , continues to value very highly. There can be no doubt as to the existence of all growing feeling in the country in favour of the Government making better provision for the widows and orphans of our soldiers, and also for soldiers and sailors permanently disabled in the service of the country. The ideal state of things would be for the Government to become molel employers, subject te the provisions of the Workmen's Compen- eation Act ; but we have not arrived even within view of all this at present. At the same time, the Government, it is only fair to say, have begun to recognise the obligation to make proper provision when the all-important ways:and means have been devised.

T 1 most people it is almost needless to say that ' what are known as the "May meetings" are as in- teresting and important to provincials as they are to resilents in London where they are held, It is gratefully recognised by the former that the reports furniqh a splendid record of work done by D3ople of all denominations, and, notwithstanding an occasional tendency to accentuate religious and political differences, they represent all that is beat and noblest in our national life. The tneetinze this year are being held under the shadow both of a war in South Africa. and of the great famine in India. The latter has a strong claim upon the sympathy of the Christian public, which appsars from reports presented by the Wesleyan and other bodies to have taken a very practical and tangible form. In India, as well as in China, English mis- sionaries have from time to time rendered valuable help to the famine-stricken people in particular districts. Foreign Missions have, as usual. loomed largely at the May meetings; as. also,hae the British and Foreign Bible Society, which has this year established another" record "in the issue of Bibles testaments, and portions of Scripture, the total reeehing the astounding figure of more than five millions. The high mission of England, spoken of by the Premier the other day, is recognised by none so fully as these organisations, and even those who do not share their zeal must admire the purity and , unselfishness of their motives. _ _

; spelling is not everything, as a member of the High worth School Board has just given other people to understand. At a meeting of the Board, the member in question handed in the following written notice of motion :—"That the Board record its appres eation of the suekesfle concert given last week by the children and school staf, in aid of a new Peannnfort for the youse of the children of the schools. That we coincide grate creddiv: is due to the Head Master Mr—and our school and staf and the children for the effont manner the drills and singing and other parts were rendered wich mad the efort such a sackess." The effort here is that of a member of the School Board not of the Board school, and setting aside the spelling as a matter of detail, does credit to the better part of the writer. When Artemis Ward said Chaucer did not know how to spell, he acknowledged that it did not pre- vent his being a good poet. In like manner, though the spelling of this particular member of a qohool Board leaves something to be deeired, he is net " above learning "or at any rate of the children being taught music and the "use of the pianoforte", at the public expense. Now that Lord Roberts has got fairly"under way' and the initial stages of the long expected advance hare been successfully accomplished, many pro- vincial towns are anticipating another outburs% of rejoicing end patriotic demonstration over the ex- pected relief of Alafeking. May they not be dis- appoieted, is the wish of us all, but if there is one saying that has been emphasised more than another in connection with the present war it is that which commences "There's many a slip—." Still there is a great deal to rejoice over in the progress which has been made by Lord ltoberts and the troops under him during the past week. The wish that is uppermost in most men's minds, however, is, that the movement now being made may bring the end of the campaign very much nearer,end if to an end, the sooner the better. Certainly, with the capture of Smaldeel and Winburg we have had eloquent proofs of the part that the Colonials can and are prepared to play in the great organisation of Imperial defence.

Judge G wynne-James held his usual Court at Runcorn on Tuesday, but it proved void of interest- i Jg public bu-iness.
RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB.

Notices of a special meeting of the members and of the general annual meeting of the above club appear in this issue to take place at Mr. Riley's Cate on Tuesday May 15th, and Tuesday May 29th respectively. See Advt.
THE ALLEGED STRANGLING OF A RUNCORN YOUTH.

Before Mr. W. Handley, at the Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday morning, Edwin Parkinson, was brou2ht up on remand charged with unlawfully and maliciously doing grevious bodily harm to a Run- corn youth named Leonard Sergeant.—The Super- intendent of Police asked for a further remand as the boy was still suffering severely from the in- juries received, and was unable to attend Court.— Prisoner was further remanded for a week. THE INDIAN FAMINE.

In response to an appeal from the Lord Lieuten- ant (Earl Egerton) and the County Council, the Runcorn Urban District Council have decided to open a local fund for Runcorn, as a branch of the Central County Fund and have issued requests to Clergymen and Ministers to arrange for taking collections at their respective churches ;to enlist the active help of the manu- facturers and employers at their respective works, and to open a special acc)unt at Paresßank for the receipt of donations. Knowing the large hearted- nees of the Runcorn public we feel sure the matter will enlist their full sympathy.

The annual re-anion and tea meeting of Mr. Simister's Wednesday Glass was held at the Bruns- wick Schools on Wednesday evening last, when about 60 members at down to a capital tea served by alesdarnes headstone, and Bisbrown. The proceeds made from the tea were given to a deserving widow. Afterwards Mr. Simister delivered a short address and address9s and players were offered by Messrs.D. Bisbrown, T Watson, S Coventry. T Boath, J Lead- stone, W Rushton, R Eaden, T T Burrows, G 11 Kirkham, E Bowden and others.—A most enjoyable qnd comforting meeting was closed with prayer by Mr G 11. Kirkham. RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD NiERTING-.

The ordinary monthly meeting of the above Board held at the Town gall Buildings, last Thurs- day nify,ht, was attended by the Rev. Canon Wood (chairman), Meesrs h unison (vice-chairman), F J Norman, 3.,1111,38 Pritchard, S Taylor, W J Cunning- ham, J Littler, and J W Lighcburn (clerk) and A Lighthurn (assistant clerk).—On the recommenda- tion of the School Management committee Miss Jessie Burton was appointed assistant-mistress at the Victoria-road Board Schools, vice Miss S Williams resigned, at a salary of .E4s.—The Board recorded its vote in favour of the Rev. Canon Wood and Mr. Wade Deacon, in the election of the Execu- tive Council of the Association of School Boards.— It was resolved on the motion of Mr. liaison, oeconded by Mr. S Taylor, that the Chairman Mr. Pritchard, and the Clerk should represent the Board at the annual meeting of the Union of Lancashire and Cheshire Institutes to be held at Blackpool next Oc oher.—Tne Board approved of the scion of the Cierk in allowing Mr. Ward, organizing secre- tary to the Technical Instruction Committee of the County Council, the use of the Board schools in Victoria-road for the purposes of the County Coun- cil Scholarships Examination. There were 45 can- didates from Runcorn and district. RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT FRODSIIAM.

.An alarming accident which might have been attended with direful results, occurred on Friday last at Froisham Junction, near Runcorn. A paqs• anger train due at Runcorn at 4 2 from Chester,was about to turn the sharp curve at this point when the en4ine left the rails on the inside, doing consider- able damage to the permanent way. The embank- ment is particularly steep, but the engine did not get beyond the inside metal, so that the only inconvenience the passengers felt was a slight shak- ing, folloived by the inevitable delay. Information was at once despatched to Runcorn, and the station- master (Ur. Prescott) on receiving the notification requisitioned an engine, and repaired t 3 the spot. Here he arranged for a single line service. The breakdown gang from Warrington, which had in the meanwhile been summoned, came upon the scene and set to work to clear the obstruction. The train was detached from the engine, taken to Froisham station, only a short distance away, and worked on the up line. The breakdown gang worked hard, and about seven o'clock had the satis- faction of getting the engine clear. They then cora- meneed to repair the permanent way, and at 10.30 the line was opened again, and traffic, which had been somewhat disorganized, was resumed. The passengers on the train reached Runcorn at 6-20 p.m. KINDNESS REWARDED —4lls. BAXTER'S LAST CHANCE.

Harriet Baxter, who is well-known both to the Rune )rn Police and magistrates, was again brought op on Friday last, c`)FargPd with wandering abroad without visible mAans of subsiQtence. She pleaded guiltv,ani t'ie case WAS proved by Acting Sergeant S Gregory —Toe magistrates reminded sirs. Baxter of the promises she had made them a few days pre- viously, when she promised to go to Manchester.— he said she was' sorry but had spent the money in drink instead. She pleaded that if the magistrates would give her another chance she would go back to the Workhouse at Dutton, and walk there that very day.—The Suparintendent being appealed to, said the prisoner had had 80 many chances, that there was no reason to believe she would go. She had broken her -promises so often.—The Bench, however, decided upon giving her a last chance,and the Chairman J Norman) very kindly paid her fare to Sotton Weaver. ASSA.ITLT ON TRH POLICE AT RUNCORN.

David Roberts, ne captain of a schooner lying at Weston Point, was fined 5s and 54 costs for being drunk and disorderly, and 20s and 53 costs for as- saulting P.C. Wilson, at Runcorn, on the 3rd of \fay.—The magistrates who imposed the penalty were Messrs. F. J. Norman and W. Ilandley.—lt appeared that Roberts was very drunk onthe night in question and was proceeding along the tow- path of the Bridgewater Canal. when Constable Wilson seeing his danger advised him to go "home" by a safer route. Roberts either was too drunk, or misinterpreted the constable's good offices for he struck the offieer a smart blow on the ear with his fist. Constable Nicholls happened to be with Wilson at the time, and Roberts next morning made the acquaintance of the magistrates with the above re- sult.—geberts, before leaving the court apologised to the constable, and thanked him for taking care of him for he really could not remember what be had done.

div.head: RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB.
div.p: RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB.
Review of the Season 1899-1900.
A Record and a Cup.

If there is one thing more ehan anotiaer that appeals to Runcorn. people, it is the references made to its footballer, and their exploits. Year after year has seen the name of Ittincorn figure promin- ently in the football world, and for a town of but some 20,000 inhabitants to be likened to a nursery Lr first-class footballers, is a distinction to be proud-of, and one that no other town can boast. On top of all its great achievements Itancorn has just closed a season ot foetball that has been one of the most brilliant in all its annals. Follow- ing up the remarkable successes that atten led the Runcorn team at the conclusion of 1893 -1899 (a , season that closed with a succession of brilliant victeries) they entered upon 1899-1900 with suck zeal and energy as to win for themselves a place at the head of the Lancashire Section of the, Northern Union —a position they retained through- out the whole season—not even OUCH stepping down for a re sal. Victorious they com- menced ; and victorious they remained, and at the close of an unparalleled competition they reaped their rev:o.rd. Eight victories heralded the fact to the outside world that Runcorn were going strongly :—Wigan, Swinton, Broughton, Widnes, Oldham, Tyldesley (twice) and Hull Kingstrn Rovers, in succession bending the knee to the prowess of the " Liunets." Then came the first bitter pill—the fall of the " mighty " at Stockport. The match recalled stands out vividly as a blot upon the (up to that time) perfect performances of the Rancorn team. But, let me draw a veil upon that miserable game ; for the victory reflected little credit upon Stockport, a circumstance which inten- sifies the discredit attached to Kuncortee share in the event. The following sixteen matches were productive of fifteen wins, and one uraw. Tais latter was brought about by the flue display of the Leigh men on their own ground on the 30;h of December. Th s teams beaten included: Stockpert and Leigh (or e), Altrinchana, Millom, Salford, RoAdale Hornets, Warrington and Wigan (twice) and St. llelens (once). Salford, Rochdale, Warring- ton and Sr. Ilel-sns affrded great games. Then came a defeat for Runcorn at the hends of St. Helens. This was mostly attributable to the fact that Runcorn had met Salford the previous Wednesday, and naturally toek the field a trifle stale. As it was St St. Helens only merseged to win by three points to two points ; and all who recall the hard lines ex- perienced by Houghton towards the end of that game when Briers scored a try through the veteran's mistake cannot but sigh over the result. Still it was no disgrace. A draw at Wid:ies was the verdic.; of the following Seturelay's play, and who did not enjoy the rare gold tussle that brought it about? Then came the event of the season: Runeern an )Idb.am meeting at Runcorn to decide the champion- ship. For Runcorn that fixture proved a decidedly happy one. Their finances, which bays for some years been in but an indifferent plight, were that day rejuvenated. £360 and over were taken in "gate," and in addition Runcorn crowned the season's achievements by vanquishing Oldham and securing the cup. This too after a game of games in which neither team showed up the worse. Few matches have surpassed it for incident and vigour, and the winners deserve every honour. Thus the close of the " competition " saw Runcorn possessed of a "pot,' and determined to go in strongly for a companion for it. Striding grandly towards the Northern Union Cup, an flushed veite their successes, Runcorn easily disposed of Birstall, Maryport and Bralford (the winners of the York- shire Section). Fate decreed that Bradford and Runcorn, should try conclusions in a tournament of three matches. These games proved a veritable struggle for "The Cock o'the North." March 31st recorded a pointless draw at Bradford, and orders to repl47 at Runcorn the following Monday caused a cheerful flutter throughout Rancorn foot- ball circles, and expectations of vlctory ran high But that meeting resulted 3-3, and hopes were mt so cheery, as Runcorn had no fresh players to ,Irn=v op)o. whilst Bradford were considered to be well off. Meeting for a third rime. however, at Broughton, Bradford were vanquished and Runcorn progressed cupwards almost confident they had their hands upon it. The Saturday followinm saw Leeds Parish Church only able to draw against Runcorn, on the Leeds ground. This, in face of the fact that already Runcorn had played 'three trying matches within the week natur- ally caused a return of confidence. Runcorn from a mistaken idea of superiority kept off four of their best mea in the return match. Oh ! the pity of it. Wednesday saw them facing Leeds at Runcora. The game progressed. Runoorn had their own way almost throughout Yet the Parishioners won, and closed Runcorn's bidding for silver plate in a manner that brought down very uncomplimentary comments upon the heads of the launcorn team. The struggle for the,' cup was, however, a brilliant one—if an unsuccessful ono—and marks Runcorn as a remarkable toam of " stayers.”—The revival of the Mist Lancashire Cun Competition saw Wigral vsnquished by 32 points to nil. Then Rune srn had the privilege of meeting S. Helen, at Widnes. in the final tie. Tthl match being hot of recent- occurrence can easily be recalled. It was remarkable for the il!-hick which dogged the steps of the Runcorn players. Farmer, Tomliason, and Langley being rendered hors de combat whilst St. Helens all marvellously escaped. The match proper resultsd in a pointless draw, though but 12 Runcornites faced the last half-hour of the music. An extra 15 minutes fol- lawied—(witb °die "15 :o 12 "in favour of the Saints) —and in the semi-darkaesa Runcorn were blotted out from that Competition. At the end of the season Run- corn faced the" Rest of Competition," and beat them too. Afterwards the presentation of the cun and medals took plaee,and it is no secret how the honours have been done to it and the Runcorn players. A. word about the players and their play. Runcorn's brilliant season has been an exhibition of what a fine defence can accomplish. Houghton is without equal as 'a back—and he has two porfeet supports in J >May anit Butterworth. In fact the whole team are a team of defenders when there is need for it. Even the forwards can play back as if by ins:lrct. Jones, C Butterworth, and the ever prominent Warder have given a good aecount of themsaves. At half-back Faulkner stands out as an attackar and to him and Jolley whose goal dropning propensHes are well knownstheereatestleortion of tne points are due. The forwards Farmer, 'Railcar, . Darlington, Langley, Taylor, 0 Hughes,Reece,Lightfoot, ; Tomliasnn. and Garter we can ,ot say too mac s of, far they have share,' a hard seasoa hetween the-fl with unparalleled credit. Woods and Diless3nger have also been eccellent reserve lads.

DEATH AND FUNERAL OF Mn. RATREI BATE.—We rec ,rd with reret the sudden death of Mr. Ralph Bate. veterinary surgeon and farmer, of Natherton, wh ch took place at his residence last Sunday.—The funeral which was largely attended, took place at the 0 Jerton Parish Church on Wednesday afternoon. During his life Ur. Bate identified himself with the public life of his district, and was at one time a churchwarden, He was also a member of the Frodsham Lordship Pariah Council.
RUNCORN NOTES. ---- [Br A. CORRESPONDENT].

The work of improving the Runcorn heath and common has practically been commenced, and Mr. James Wilding has already got completed the principle drainage service which connects the heath and common with the town system. This is naturally a costly operation, and as the money is to a certain extent" buried" the public will not see ve7 mach for it, What they can see, however, is the work that is being carried out in the way of roael.-making, awl this is a work that even the most selfish must think highly of.

Other improvements to our town are the well- executed repairs to Greenway-road,Dactor's Bridge, Church-street and High-street. That they were necessary is beyond question ;and we are all thank fulfto :,ee the necessity attended to. Whilst dealing with town's affairs, however, I should like to call attention to the side entries, and alleys-7-that are ostensibly private, though, of course, used by the public generally. Seldom or never do any of them feel the effscts of a" clean sweep," though, in the interests of the public health, they sadly need one. The Health Committee of the Runcorn Urban DIE, trict Council have accomplished some useful work, and calling Mr. Dean's attention to this subject I feel sure will result in some practicll remedy.

St. Paul's—or rather the Old Brunswick Sunday School—commemorates its centenary this year. I hear the occasion is going to be fittingly observed and Wesleyans in the town are going to put for- ward tbeir utmost eff,rts to make it a red letter day in the history ot Nonconformity in Runcorn. None ctn praise too highly the good and holy work these ancient schools have accomplished, and it is to he hop-sd those who have benefited by its erection will flock to it, and render it such support, that" Old Brunswick" may for centuries to come flpurish and prosper in its sphere of usefulness, It is the mother of all the Nonconformist Churches in the district and though many of her children are jealous of her, may they use this occasion for a happy reunion.

The action of the Runcorn Board of Guardians in deciding to be guarantors for the blind children which the Runcorn School Board are compelled to relinquish, is one that makes ratepaying a cheerful occupation, Of all rates the Poor Rata is the oge we mlst cheerfully pay; and we are always more gratified when we heir that the poor are to benefit a little by it.

The Tralsporter Bridge pronalt3ra have agreed in tote to the wishes of the Rural District Council, regarding the undertaking for thE transportation of hay, and the farmer sees no further cause for obje,ctian to the bridge. Personally. I am only sorry the Cheshire and Lancashire County Councils, the Widnes Town Council, and the Runcorn Urban District Council did n3t put their heads together in the first instance, as I advised, and consider the question of a bridge— Transporter or otherwise—that wauld be free from all objection and meeting their views and erect it themselves at the public coit. A passage across the Nlersey is S 3 important, at this point, that it should be as free and accessible as the King's highway. But though sorry tor this omission on their part, I bow to the inevitable.

French Balloon found near Warrington.

On Tue-dav morning, at about ten o'clock, a somewhat large balloon tell in the field of Mr, Flnrcon.Little Lsigh.between Warrington and North- wich, creating considerable interest. Mr. Seater, engineer of the electric railway, examined it and found instructions in French and German for the balloon to be returned to th,i Observatory, Trappe, France. A meeting of the above committee- was held on Mon- day, April 23d. It was resolved that Mr. Thompson be chairman of the committee for the etsoing year. Tne Clerk reported, as instructed at the last meeting, with reference to the claim of Mr Isaac Wloittle,of Earle-street of the sum of £2 103 6 I for damages alleged by him to have been caused by falling over gas mains in Earle- street, and stated that after investigation he was of opinion that the claim was fair and reasonable, where- upon it was resolved that Mr. Isaac Whittle b. paid the sum of £2 103 61 in full se•tlement of his Waif . A letter dated the 4th of April, 1900, W 39 read from Mr. G. Airey, of Sandfield hail, Lowton, applying for a gas supply to a gas engine at his house. The Clerk reported that he had written to the Corporation of Leigh asking their permission to lay a gas main within their area of supply, but that as their Gas Committee had not vet met he had had no definite answer, whereupon it was resolved that subject to the cousent being given by the Leigh Corporation the application of Mr. Airey be acceded to.—A :fitter from the sc.,kers at the gasworks applying for eight hour shifts insteal of 12,as at present, was referred to the Gas-works Extensions Committee for their coesidera.tion and report. The miout3s were confirmed on the mstioa of Mr. Thompson seconded by Mr Beatty. WATER COMMI r TEE.

The Clerk was instructed to suitably reply thereto.—A letter datei the 24th of March, 1900, was read from Mr F W Webb, engineer of the London and North-Western Railway Comp my at Crewe,enclosing therewith a formal notice on behalf of the Railway Com- pany to the District Council stating that it was the inten- tien of the Company, on and after the 30th day of Sept., 1900, to put an end to the arraneetnent. at present exist- ing whereby they supply the C )(mil with water, and that accordingly on tha date mentioned the supply would be di3continued.—L4ters dated the 29th of March,l9oo, and the 3rd of April, 1900, were read from Mr John Thom, contractor for the boreholes, with reference to the completion of his cantract. Smith stated that at 2.30 on tee previous; afternoon he was on duty at the Police Station when he received a complaint about disorderly conduct in Aikin-street. THE TREATMENT OF BLIND CHILDREN. LENGTHY CORRESPONDENCE.

Mr. Thomas Taylor, superintendent of the School for the Blind, Herdmars-,t.eet, Liverpoel wrote under date 30th April, with reference to Elizebeth Whittaker, and Zechariah Hughes "The above children, now pupils in our branch school will attain the age of 16—Whittaker on the 24th June and Huelms en the Bth May,—and therefore their guerantors (tne Runcorn &Moot Board) will cease to be liable for their payments on those dates. Will you kindly ask your board to become guarantors for them and sign tee encloted form of agreem2nt, and thus enab!e the children to be transferred to th 3 school where they will be te.ught the means of earning a lived- hoot You will observe the terms are Els per week ; clothing extra." The Clerk said he had been in communication with the Clerk to the Runccen School Board, and had re- ceived from him the following letter:— Town Hall. Waterioo-road, Runcorn, Bth May, 1900. Dear Sir re Zaehariah Hughes.—l wrote to the superin- tendent ot the Liverpool School for the Bind stating that the Guardians would probably refuse to make a payment on behalf of this boy,and that the father woull also refuse to pay the amount required, the result being that the boy would be taken to his father's house. I further described the nature of this home. Under the circumstances, I suggested that the authorities of the Blind School should find the boy employment as a teacher, or irk some other way, in consideration for his services. At the present time this boy plays the organ at the Blind School Gavel, and is much respected in the institution. I euclose the reply to this communica- tion. I have bad an interview with the father who is willing to pay 31 per week khalf the cost), end provide elothea fnr his son. This is tie extreme limit to which the father will go—the alternative being to keep the boy II at home. lam sir, yours truly, John W. Lightburn. George F. Ashton, E•q. Mr. Lightburn received the following reply to his letter .—" To Mr. Jelin W. Light. burn, Town Hail, Runcorn, Dear Sit :re Zechariah Hughes. In reply to your letter of the 5:41 lam sorry to inform you that we have not a vacancy for another monitor at VVavertree Branch School. I hope the Guardians will pay fur the boy and send le'm here as I should be eorry for him to go wrong as he soon would de at the age he now is if he had bad advisers. Kindly do your best for him and so oblige, yours faithfully THOMAS TeeLoa, superintendent." Mr. Meadowcrolt said the father of this boy worked at the deck, and the cise :tame under his notice that morning before he left. The father requeeted his fore- man to speak to him (Mr. Meadowcroft) snout the case as he expected the matter wou'd ceme before the Guar- dians that day. From whet he heard the boy seemed to. him to be an intelligent boy, and a sample of his writing was shown to trine which he thought spoke much tor his qualifications. H;s father and mother were in the Court only a short time ago, and their borne was no the place for a boy who had such good qualifications and such a good conduct record. Be did not think he should be lerceight home and left to the tender mercies of big parents. If it was really in order for that Board to assist to the rxr.ent they were asked to do. he certainly thought it was a case where they might reehteouelv do so. He thou :he the father was making an offer to contribute towards the boy's maintenance, and if ha carried out his intention he should certainly think better of him.
The Clerk raid the cost would be six shillings per week for each cAee. and ia the case of the boy they expeetod to receive three sivlliGge pr week towards his maintenince.
The Baird decided to become guarantors for the chit. deco in accordance witn '.115 request of the Superintend- ent's letter.

DARESBURY SCHOOL BOARD. The Education of—M—r—Weir's Children.

The monthly meeting of the Daresbury School Board was held in:the Board Room last Thursday afternoon, when there were present the Rev. H.T. Clarke (chair- man), Messrs. Phillips, Cooper, Warbarton, Weir, Bill- ington, and Sharp (assistant clerk).
SALARIES INCREASED. The Chairman moved and it was unanimously, agreed that the sa.!aries of the two monitoreases be increased from £2 101. to £4 per annum.

MR. WEIR'S CRILDREN. It may be remembered that at the last meeting of the Board Mr Weir brought forward the matter of the education of his two children, who are deaf and dumb. One of the children is at the Old Trafford Deaf and Dumb School, Manchester, and the Board contribute £8 6s 8d per annum towards his education, Mr Weir paying for the child's maintenance and clothing. He now desires to send his other child to the institution, and asks that the Board should pay for it education the sum of £lO 6s 8d per annum,which, he contends, they are legally bound to pay. At the meeting in question the Clerk (Mr. Linaker) said the Board were Under no obligation to contribute to the cost of educating either of the children, but they could grant any sum if they chose up to a certain limit, which was prercribed in the code of the education department. The matter was adjourned in order that the Clerk might write to the Education Department asking what amount, if any, the Board was bound to pay for the education and maintenance of the child at Old Trafford.

On Tcursday the Assistant Clerk stated that the reply of the education department was to the effect that the Board could contribute to the child's education/any sum up to £l5, according to the circumstances of the parent or guardian. The Assistant Clerk also gave some particulars as to the cost of education and maintenance at the school, from which it appeared that the total cost per week was 10s-3s 6d for maintenance and 61 6d for education. _ _ _

Mr. Cooper said the Board heartily sympathised with Mr and Mrs Weir, but as the same time they had to consider the ratepayers, and in his opinion the sum asked by Mr Weir was too large. Mr. Wear: I know tne money lam entitled to is LIO 6s Bd,and that I shall claim. The Chairman : The question is what proportion of the sum required can Mr Welr afford to pay. Mr. Philips said that was the point. An arrangement would have to ba arrived at between the Board an d the parent as to what each should pay, and the Bum tbe Board would pay would depend upon what the parent could afford te contribute. If they failed to agree, the matter should be referred to arbitration.
Eventually the Chairman moved that the Board con- tribute the same sum towarOs the education of the second cluld as was coutributed in the case of the other.
Mr. Weir . I otnnot agree to 0-mt. as lam payiog £2 more than I ought to he tyiyini for the education of tho child at present in the institution. After further disca93ion,

Mr. Cooper propoaed that the matter be further ad- journed to give Mr. Weir an opportunity ef bringing evidence, if posaible, that the Board was comrrlled to pay the whole sum required for the child's education. Mr. Phillips seconded, and tho motion was agreed to. There was no other business of public interest.

div.head: trttersto tbe attar.
div.p: trttersto tbe attar.
The Ragged School Bazaar and Fete.—A Protest Against Gambling.

Sir,—A circular letter concerning the Bazar about to be held on bele Of of the Warrington Undenorninational Ragged Sehool has just Grine under my notice. I venture to think it calls for serious and emphatic pro- test. A gold watch value £lB will be awarded to the person whose name appears opposite or nearest to the Second at which the watch will have stopped after the Mayor has wound it on June 11th. The public are in- vited to put their names at any and all of the 43,200 seconds which make up the watch's course of twelve hours, at the price of one penny per signature. This methed of raising money is as creditable to the ingenuity of its deviser as it is discreditable te the organisation which employs it. The promoters calmly announce that if all the 720 sheets are filled with signatures, the EitlM of £lBO will be raised on an article they themselves value at £lB only. The preposterous audacity of such a propcsal is indeed staggering. Com- mend me rather to the organisers of sweepstakes on the next horse race ! Here is an invitation to a person to try and gain fer a penny what the community at large has staked £lBO for. In other words, it is a flagrant instance of the sin and selfishness of gambling, whose inward motive is the desire to possess oneie self of the property of another without rendering any adequate return. But this is by no means the worst feature of this lamentable exhibition. For all this, forsooth, is being done bv, and on behalf of an organisation whose whole raison d'être is gone,if it does not tend to elevate the community among which it works. If our moral light be darkness, bow great ie that darknefe ? The national vice of gambling and betting is growing to quite alarming proportions. And yet our religious organisations—and in justice albeit with great respec, I have to charge the Church of England with olten being an arch offender—instead of strenuously and earnestly combating this evil, are weakening whatever protest they may make against the more glaring forms of gambling, by themselves partici- pating in the accursed thing. Thus we prove the truth of Schiller's lament: "And money rules as God of the earth." Does its grotesque inconsistency, I wonder. never strike the promoters of such a gambling concern? The moral, as the physical lever has three forces acting upon it. The first is the moral and spiritual Power which is ever seeking to manifest itself in the world. The second is the resistance of evil which all right minded people desire to see overcome. The third is the moral fulcrum upon which the lever works. And religious organisations form, I suppose the chief part of Ms moral fulcrum. Now, every mechanic knows that if the fulcrum be flabby and weak, the power exerted will fail to overcome the resisting force. When will the religious mechanic leers the suns truth concerning moral leverage? To my mind few things in life are more sec], and yet at the same time more absurd than the employment, often by really well-iis- posed people,of immoral means to gain some moral end. The attempt is not only futile. but even worse, for it accelerates the forces of evil and strengthens their power of resistance. May I also, with all respect, remind our worthy Mayor of what the Noncenformist Dr. Clifford has recently said, that while drink was the great cause of ruin in the past it is now gambling anti betting ; and may I funher zemind him that in promoting such a lottery as this he is breaking the law of the land he is called upon to administer. If I were a Chief Constable I would rigor- ously prosecute all organisers of oizears who thus flag- rantly violate morality and law. To those of my fellow Churchmen who see ns harm in raffling and sush forms, of the gambling which i 3 spelling ruin to thausands of charactcrs and homes I would suggest reflection on a saying ef S, Clemens Alexandrinus, "Idleness and wantonness provide these games for the lazy and useless people of the world."—Yours etc , FRANCIS E. POWELL.
S. James' Vicarage+, May 3rd, 1900.

div.head: NEW POLICE COURT
div.p: THE NEW POLICE COURT
AT NEWTON.
Opening on Thursday.

The new Police Court which has been erected at New- ton was used for the first time on Thursday. Before the commencement of the business, Mr. H. J. Longton said that he did not know whether, before commencing the business of the Court in that new building, it wolid be opportune and proper for him as the senior member of the local bar to congratulate the Bench on the possession and a quisition of that new and handsome building. There was no deubt that it WdS a well constructed building so far as be was able to judge and he hoped it would be convenient and suit- able for all the requirements that it would have to meet. It had, however, seemed to him, casually epeaking,that the courtroom was rather small for the business which was very considerable at the Newton Police Court on so many occasions. Perhaps they had been accommodated with an extra large room before and they might become accustomed to the smaller accommodation that obtained there. He hoped that the Chairman wculdbe often present at the Court and would administer justice in the same fair and impartial manner that be had always dene in the past, and that the publ,c might if possible he better accommodated in that building than they had been in the other one. The solicitors' bench did not seem to be a very large one and the superintenden's were necessarily in attendance there. He hoped they might fit themeelvea to that inconvenience as time progressed and that they might dud it to be suitable.Mr Longton also offered the congratulations of the solicitors to Mr. Colliagwood on his appointment to the Bench. They hoped he would be as good a magistrate as his predecessor,if be might be allowed to put it in that was. If he was such he would give great satisfaction,not oely to his colleagues and to the solicitors but also t 3 the epubtic at large. er The Chairman (Mr. T. J. Gillespie), said that the 'building was certainly a very great improvement on the , old Town Hall, and he thought they would avoid many colds that they used to gat from that draughty old plzc Mr. LoLgton rightly said that the Court was a little smaller than the 'old Town Hall, but no doubt the 'authorities bad considered the improving condition of the country, and had thought a smaller court would meet the exigencies' of the case. The court was very mush better for the reason that it was nee draughty like the old hall. In conclusion he expressed the hope thae the harmonious manner in which the business bad always been conducted would still continue. The business was then proceeded with. DESCRIPTION OF THE BUILDINGS.

"'The new buildings cover 1,275 yards, about two thirds of which represent the area allotted for main buildings, and the remainder for a yard and an outbuilding,which will be used as a weights and measures office for the township of Newton-le-Willows. The courtroom is smaller than that previously used, but it has a much more comfortable appearance. The space granted to the public is very Ihnited,and probably not more than thirty Parsons are able to gain admittance. The windows are of stained glass,and in the centre of 000' in the county coat-of-arms. The wood used throughout is satin walnut. Hot water coils and pipes heat the room, as also all the other large Pantos: Oa the entrance to the magistrates' bench is placed an over door in the centre of which is engraved the county coat-of-Arms. The magistrates' consulting room, which will also be used as extra court room when necessary, is in ttie rear of the magistrates' bench. The public entrance to the court is on the north a the building, and adjoining this is a staircase leading', to three double cella,the dimensioni of which are-14 feet by I feet. The doors are of iron casting fitted with spring locks. Residences are provided for the sergeant and a con- stable on the north lard south side of the buildings, and the charge office lies between these houses. The bricks used in the building are of Accrington make, and the stone facings are from Collingworth, Yorkshire. The contractor is Mr. John Dicken.on, of Westhoughton, Balton, and the architectural designs are by the County Coun3il's architect, Mr. Henry Littler, Areston. Thn cost of the buildings is roughly estimated at between £5,000 and £6,000.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

INDIAN FAMINE RELIEF FUND.—On Saturday afternoon a May-Queen procession was formed for the purpose of assisting the• Mayor's Indian Famine Fund. Twenty girls and boys drosied in appropriate costumes parade 1 Whitefield-road, Walton-road, Bedford-street, London- road,and Birchdale,salling on their way at the residences of Mr Robert Davies, Mr Henry Greenall and Mr Monk 3 and also at the Lawn Tennis Ground. The girls, avh) were dressed in white costume 3 carried bouquets of flowers and the boys wore military costumes. National flags were carried, and the procession generally had a very pretty appearance. •The May Queen was Diey Moir, her train bearers being Margery Muir and Ethel Mclntyre. The Maids of Honour were Kithleen Barker and Annie Laurie. The collectors, who used fancy tam- bourines, were Edith Bonnell, Marion England and Barbara Laurie. Tre procession was planned and ar- ranged by Miss Elith B mnell with the assistanc of Mrs Frank Warburton. The amount collected was £2 12.
