div.head: WAR.
div.p: THE WAR.
LATEST TELEGRAMS.
The British Advance Across
Zand River.
Message from Lord Roberts. Lord Roberts to the Secretary of State for War :
WELGELEGEN, MAY 9TII, 7 P.M.
Pole-Crow's and Tucker's divisions, lan Hamil- ton's column, the heavy Naval and Royal Garrison Artillery guus,and four Brigades of Cavalry marched here to-day. _
The enemy hold the opposite: bank of the Zand River.
Their strength will be ascertained to-morrow, when I hope to be able to force the passage of the

river. Message cabled from the cable cart, Fleadquar- ters, Front, May 10, 9-10 a.m. We are Row across Zand River. Enemy still holding strong position, but we are gradually pushing them back. Enemy in Full Retreat. The following telegram from Lord Roberts was posted at the War Office yesterday : Cable Cart, Zand River, 10th May. Enemy in full retreat. 4,Tney occupied a position 20 miles in length. Ours was necessarily longer, .with widely scat- tered forces.
Boer War News. Acknowledgment of Defeat. An Amazon Army. PRETORIA, WEDNESDAY.

The following war bulletin has been issued The British took possession of Fourteen Streams on Sunday. The bombardment was so heavy that the Federals were forced to retire. The retreat was accomplished in good order. At M.afeking thirty-two horses have been cap- tured. A female burgher has telegraphed to the Presi- dent stating that she is prepared with a body of women volunteers to take up arms in defence of their independence. The War Drawing to a Close. Impending Annexation of the Free State. CAPE TOWN, THURSDAY. The " Argu3 " consiJers that the Boer defence is 011apsing, and that the war is drawing to a speedy close. It is believed that a proclamation annexing the Free State will be issued when the Vaal is reached.

div.head: OUR GALLANT VOLUNTEERS.
div.p: OUR GALLANT VOLUNTEERS.
Warrington's Second Con- tingent for the Front, DINNER AT THE TOWN HALL.

The second contingent of the let Prince of Wales Volunteers South Lancashire Regiment. con-istine of a Lieutenant and 20 men, who have volunteered for active service,were entertained to dinner at the Town Hall on Monday evening. His Worship, the Mayor, presided over the proceedings, which were of an enjoyable character. During the evening the men were presented with field glasses and policies insuring them for £lOO. together with a prayer card from the Rector, photo- graphically ill-astrated by Mr. T. Births. In addition to the Mayor and the Volunteers, there were present the Rev John Yonge ( Mayor's Chaplain), the Rev Canon Willis, Mr F Monks, .T.P., C.C., Alderman Fairclough,J.P,, Councillor A Bennett Major toome (adjutant of the Volunteers), Major Buckton,Alderman and Captain Hutchinson,Captain Walters, second Lieutenant Carey (commanding the service contingent), Mr J L Whittle (town clerk), Mr John Fairhuret (borough treasurer), and the editors of the local newspapers. Mr. Po wis catered and when the company had settled down to the en- joyment of coffee and cigars, The MAYOR proposed in very fitting terms the usual loyal toasts. These were enthusiastically honoured, the" National Anthem " and " God Bless the Prince of Wales" being sung. Mr. PEARSE then sang with vigour the popular "Soldiers of the Queen." Councillor BENNETT proposed "The Bishops, clergy and all ministers of religion," who, he re- marked were in spite of differences, all one. Recent events had shown them that, although in ordinary times of peace and comfort their political and national differences were very marked, at a time of real stress and difficulty all these differences melted into thin air and all became Englishmen and patriots. He almost wished there could be a similar common danger to threaten the religious world. (Laughter.) It was difficult to imagine an attade upon their religion, but he was sure it would result in the disappearance of religious disputes in the same way as the war had swept away the differ- ences that existed at home and in the various parts of the empire. (Hear, hear.) With this toast were coupled the names of the Rector and the Rev. John Yonge. They had learnt to respect and love the Rector, who had gained the admiration and homage of the whole town. (Applause) The Rev. John Yonge had identified himself with everything that promised to be advantageous to the town, and he had earned a respect and regard that was only ac- centuated as years went by. Neither could claim the high title of being a Warringtonian ; but al- though not Warringtonians born,they'were annexed Warringtonians, and as good as any others. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) After the toast had been honoured, and Mr. F. &won had sung" Weuld you like to go halves in this P" The Rev. Canon WILLIS, its respowe, said he looked upon the toast as a sign that Englishmen. and English soldiers,were not ashemed of their religion and that they regarded with affection those who ministered to their spiritual needs. Alter alluding in complimentary terms to the late Bishop of the Diocese and his successor, the Rector went on to speak abeut the war. He said he regarded these men whie were going to Africa with the greatest interest and sympetny. Their little mistake at the Parish Church on the previous night he thought would show them that they had a deer. interest in the welfare of those engaged in the war, for they com- menced ringing the tells, beceuse thee thought that Mafeking had been relieved. (Laughter ) He was only sorry that he was not present at t!se Parish Church on Sunday morning when, he was informed, they were there, but he had made other arrang,ments that cuild not be changed. The Church regarded these rnen.as he bad said, with interest and sympathy, and he was sure they would value their affection and would like to know the deep conviction that he felt that the co untry was engaged in a righteous war, and, as he believed in the bottom of his heart, a necessary war. (Hear, hear.) He spoke on the authority of such a man as tbe late Bishop of Bloemfontein,who was bishop for fißeen years and whose opinion—that there never would be true and lasting peace and happiness in Africa until the Boers, had:been thoroughly beaten—had been approved by all authorities. He knew this Bishop, for they were at college together, and he was one of the gentleale kindest, ablest and manliest of men. He rowed in his boat, was a success at his college, was the holiest of men, and that was his testimony as to the war. (Applause ) He was aura the men composing the contingent would not forget their religion. He believed that the most religious men were really the bravest men, and the bravest men were often religious leen. He had received a 1-tter frons Sergeant Ray, who was in the 3rd South Lancashire Reeiment at Colesberg, who told him that he had made a point of attending church regularly and enclosed a very beautiful hymn which he asked should be sung, if possible, at the Parish Church. He had arranged to hive it sung at next Sunday's services. They would not far- I get their religion he was sure, because they had to face death in the field or from sickness, and they should be prepared. Mr Birtles had again most kindly printed the little cards with. the colours of the Regiment and a prayer upon them, and he asked each man to accrpt one as a little gift that evening. Hs thanked Mr. Bennett for the kind way in which he had spoken of him .and the

company for the manner in which they had received the toast. (Applause.) T 0.3 Rev, Jon' YONGE said he joined with the Rector in thanking them for the reception of the toast, and in baLking Councillor Bennett for his kind Allusions. He had described both of them as annexed Wairingtooians, which was a novel iiea. (Laughter.) Although it was true that in the street sense of the word he was not a ' Warriugtonian he had been with them for nearly 24 years, and he could sae, without any mental reservation whatever, that the length of residence he had now been permitted to enj sy there had closely ct ached him to Warrington and its institutions and all its welfare. (Applause.) It was a vary proud thing for them to know that so many of Warrington's sons were williug to go f irtti in this emergency. They gave a good hearty send- off a few weeks ago to the first batch of WarriaWon men to go, and they were now endeavouring to show the second contingent that they wore carrying from War- rington the hearty respect and the good wishes of all their fellew townsmen. They prayed that it would please G e.l to bring them back safe and sound. Nothing would give them greater satisfaction than to know that the , war bad come te a speedy and happy termination so that an honourable peace could be established in that part of the world. The successful termination of the war was she only way in which suck a peace could come ab tit. (Applause.) Mr. F. MONKS proposed "The Navy, Army, and Reserve Forces" and said he was very glad t) be there that evening to bear his teatimeay to the courage of the men who had volunteered for the front. They looked back with pride at the achievements of the Navy and the Army, over a long series of years. They could not make the Army braver, but he thought tie admin- istrative departments of the Army might be overhauled, to m.ke it still more efficient. (Applause) Be regarded the Volunteer movement as the very backbone of our national independence. With reference to fighting, he nad always believed in doing the best they could before they got into a fight,and mesa, it they got into a fight, to do the best they could. (Hear,hear.) Taere was an old electioneering maxim, "Vote straight and vote often," which he would para- phrase for those who were going to the front into "Shoot straight and shoot often." (Applause.) He was glad to think that they needed no encouragement to do their duty,and to feel that they,along with the men they would fine in Africa, inceraing the Colonials, were fully determined to make the Boers" sit up." (Applause ) The toast having been drus.k with enthusiasm, Mr. Pearse sang" The Abient-minded Begger." Major ROOME, replying, said the appreciation of the ssrvices of the Navy, Army, and Reserve Forces, which was always shown, had a greater eff et than perhaps they thought upon those who did the ceure'ry's work in the field. The toast had taken its present form for some years,but he thought in future they would have to alter in to " the Navy and Army." The question was : Where are the Reserve forces today P Seeking as a lu:este:an, ee said there was no reserve about their Warrington men, who came forward in crowds to ge to the front ; and they knew the Yeomanry and the Reserv:sts did the same. (Applause.) The MAYOR real the following telegrams an letters from teore wh s had been unable to acceet his invita- tion to he present.

Mr. R. Pierpoint telegraphed :—" Regent-street.— rhanks for invitation roueived coda. Greatly regret I cainot he with you this evening. I wish secular de- taehme t volunt ers God speed." Winn I R,dgway telegraphed from L'andudno S ;rry illness prevents 2113 11-ing with you. With yrsti p'eAsant evening and Lieutenalt Carey and men good voyage and ade re' urn 0 Old E Colonel Spratt, in a letter from Orford Birracks re- qretted that he was unable to accept the kind ilavita- thn.

In a let4r from Orford Barracks, Captain Jacob pre- sented his compliments to his Worship the Mayor, and begged to thank him for his kind invitation to dinn-r, but owing to indisposition he much regretted that he was umable to accept it. A•communication bona Mr. E. Pierpeint read:—"Marl- field, Latchfori. Dear Sir.—l am desired by f ather to 4.4 y that he regrets his inability to be present at the Volun eers' dinner to-night owing to prior engagement.— Yours truly, E. PIERPOINT." Mr. Emson sang "Is there anything else you'd like ?"

div.head: • – – • • • 9 – 01;;ir • • • A ik • • A 1.-. z , „ . , , "
div.p: The Toast of the Evening.—"Warrington's
Patriotic Sons."

The MAYOR proposed the toast of the evening, coupl- ing with it the names cf tenutenant Carey and Major Suckton. Although he did not always agree with the views of the Rsctor, he must say he did entirely agree wj'h the remarks that had fallen from his lips with r'- gird to the jus ice of this war. (Applause.) Toe Rector drecv his authority from a very estimable and worthy member of his own Church ; and he, to some extent, took his authority from the equally csimelele Church to which ne had the honour to belong. Be attached much impertance to thc's opinion of the son of the prince of African missionaries—Moffat, whose name had been a household word for a couple of generations at least, and to the statements made by members of the Congrega- tional and Free Churches in South Africa. Tbe opinions ' of these men had great weight with him, but he had. hi I addition, studied to some extent the opinions emanating from other people in South Africa, and he was boiled to come to the cenclusion that sooner or later, the war was inevitable, and that if the supremacy of the Queen and the inviolate integrity of the Empire were to be maintained the steps they were now tak- ing were unavoidable. (Hear, hear, and applause.) At tke last meeting of that kind it would be remembered that he ventured to suggest that events were likely to move rapidly teciuse Warrineton Volunteers were going to the front. Well, it was a most singular fact that events had moved rapidly. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) They had had Kimberley and Ladysmith relieved, and so recsntly as the previous night there were rumours of the relief of Mefeking, lareely owing, he believed,to the report having, got abroad that a second lot of Warring- ton men were going to the front. (Cheers and laughter.) There was more in this than appeared on the surface be- cause, as teey knew, the South Lancashire noel hii a magnificent reputation. Its description as "The Fighting Fortieth" had gone before it to South Africa, and the reputation emblazoned on its colours had been more than maintained by the gallantry and bravery of its men. (App:ause.) That was the regiment to which their men belonged ; that was the regiment they were more than likely to join. Thsy were proud of the South Lancashire Regiment—(cheers)—and they were proud of the men who were being sent to it in South Africa— (epplanse)—the men who were going out to join their comrades in the task of bringing about that consumma- tion which everybody devoutly hoped would be speedily accomplished. -There was another thing which made that evening most interesting. It was held amongst all sections of her Moje.sty's subjscts that the Irishmen in the Qieen's Army had conducted thsmselves second to none in this war. (Applause.) The deeds they hid done had called forth from the Queen and from her subjects expressions of admiration that were well de- served and were most delightedly given by all who gave expression to their feelings. Therefore if anything could add to the interest they felt in those proceedings it was the feet that the contingent they were now sending out was to be led by an Irishman. (Loud cheers.) In s me renoects he hoped that their men might get to South Africa in time. but it did seem to him that events were moving very rapidly. The tremendous mobility of the Boers appeared to be developing quite in the right direction of late. (Laughter and applause.) As on more than one occasion, they might hays underestimated the Boer gift of mobility—in the way of trekking in the right direction this time. People did not like to accuse an enemy of cowardice, but he would tray that it did seem to him that the Boers appeared to be appreciating the situation (should he say) in a suitable manner ?—(loud laughter and applause)—and if their men were not speedily at the front they would have very little to do. Whether this was so or not they did know that the men they were seneling from Warrington would be as earnest as ceuraeenus, as obedient to duty, and as loyal to the Queen and the important interests of the Empire as ally of the men who had preceded them. (Cheers.) Ho would just say in conclusion that should they have to send more men—though he hoped in God's Providence they would not have to do so—he knew that to spirit and feeling of his fellow townsmen was such that the men would be forthcoming. (Applause.) Tie had every c ,n- -filence—he always had had—is the men at the head of affairs in South Africa in spite of the mistakes that had sometimes been made. A section of the Press had trial to make out that our Generals had merited severe critic- ism, but if one thing hai gratified him more than an- other it wee that these criticisms—these unjust criticisms in many casts—(hear, hear)—bad not been given utter- ance to in the provincial press. They had been largely confined to the London Press (but not all), which was now as solid and level-beaded in its management as the provincial press was well-known to be. (Hear, hear.) They wished the men of this company and Lirutenant Carey a We and comfortable voyage, a short, sharp, and smart expsrienee. and a happy return in perfect safety to the town which honoured them that night, which %Yule] honour them all the time tkey were out, and whicli would welcome them when they returned in such a manner as would compensate them for their troubles and " hardships whilst out. (Applause.) Ho coup'el with the toast the name of their leader, whom they were glad to have had the privilege of welcoming, and their own townsman, Major Buckton, who had worked so much in the interests of the battalion.

The toast 9,413 drunk to the singing of "They are jolly good fellows." Lieutenant CAREY feelingly responded. He thanked them on behalf of his men and himself for the kind speeches which had been made, and the way in which their health and FRICCESSi had been drunk. He w mld undertake that his men should not bring discredit to their regiment. (Applause.) He felt particularly proud that he was an Irishman, and that, as such, tan was p.oinc, to lead an English volunteer detac'ament—(chrerp)— although there were several ether officers much better known t the regiment who mi,?.ht have been chosen. He felt it as a greet honour paid to him. (Applause.) _ _ _

Allyn BIICXTON also r-spanded. He said t,,e highest praise should lr meted out to the men who actually went on foreign service, but all the men in the Battalion would be prepared to do their duty in liko manner were

they called upon to serve the Qneen. The whale tows, From tie Mayor, had teen the deepest interest in the Battalion. He did not knew that they deserved all the patting on the back that they had reeeivei, but the 83 men that they bad sent to the war were samples of what they could produce. As to Lieutenant Carey, they had not known him very long, but since be was introduced to them they had known him very well and learnt to appreciate him. (Hear, hear.) He had ssen a letter from Captain Appleton. dated E andslaagte, April 8:h, in which it was stated that the Warrington volunteers were getting very near the danger zotle.a.3 the Boer shells could be seen bursting. it, therefore, loon das though there was a good time coming for tnem—(laughter)— and a hot time of it for the Boers. ( kpplause.) 139 believed ally hai met with a sincere welcome from the Ist Battalion, with whom any body of men might be ' proud to he associated. (Applause.) Departure of Volunteer Drafts from Warrington.

At shout five o'clock this (Friday) morning no flwer than 16 drafts of Volunteers left Warrington for Wool- wich en route for South Africa. Each dratt consisted of 20 men and an officer so that it will be seen that the do tachments numbered in the aggregate over 300 men They were drawn from the who!* of the north-western military district and comprised the following regi- ments :

Ist South Lancashire Regiment. Liverpool Regiment. Royal Irish Regiment. Cheshire Regiment. East Lancashire Regiment. Border Regiment. North Lancashire Regiment. Royal Lancaster Regiment. M•nchester Regiment. N,-)rch Staffordshire Regiment. South S'affordshire Regiment. Royal Warwickshire Regiment. Worcestershire Regiment. Shropshire .Light Infantry. Lancashire Fusiliers. Welsh Fusiliers.

At 2 45 a.m. the men partook of brad and cheese and coffee, and at three o'clock fell in on the Barracks square. They then marched to Bink Quay Station heads(' oy the hand of the Ist South Lancashire Regi- ment, and despite the early hour a large number of p-ople eongrezated in the streets to accord them a hearts. send-',ff. Many relations and friends of those 't ordered .iuth " had come a considerable distance to bid them farewell. At various points along the route flags and bunting were displayed. Lieutenant Whitcombe, of the Woree.ter B...giment, was in commani of the whole of the detachtnenti. At the railway station the man received a hearty send-off.
REPORTED RELIEF OF MAFEKING Extraordinary Scenes at Warrington.

Extraordisare scenes were witcessed in Warrington shortly after 8 o'clock on Sunday night wh-n a rumour was circulated to the effnc that Mafeking had been relieve& The Parish Church bells rang a merry peal and in a very short space of time flags were displayed in many of the streets and n' large crowd collected around the General Post Office eagerly awaiting the display of a telegram announcing the news. Processions were formed, and the" Soldiers of the Queen " and other patriotic songs were sung, interspers d with cheers. People c mtinned to crowd round the Post Office until about 10.30. Still there were no signs of any telegram and .a heavy down- pour of rain commencing they quickly dispersed. There was great dhappointment on Monday morning,when the truth was known, and this to some extent detractfd from the effect of the real good news. In St. Helens Earlsatown and Newton similar demonstrations took' place.

Send-off at Messrs. Naylor's Works

A large number of the employ of Mesas. R. A. Naylor and Co , timber merchants, of Rowley, assembled in the Temperance Hall attached to the works, on Sloe- day evening, for the purpose sif according a hearty send- off to Private William Vernon, one of the Warrington Volunteers included in the second contingent. Private Vernon was a joiner in the employ of the firm and his fellow workmen had ‘ubserle te present him with a purse with a note book attached and about £7 in money. —William Nano, foreman of the joiners' department, presided, and asked Mr. Naylor to mike the presenta- tion.—Mr. R. A. Naylor 8414 they had met to wish one of their follow-workmen " God-speed" in the duties he had undertalson. Vernon had been with them a number of years, and possessed a very clean record and a good reputation for sobriety, honesty, and industry. Re svas now going to the front, and he torik with him their very best wishes, and he had no doebt that he would come back with as good a reputation as a soldier as the one he had had with them as a wJrkman. (applause.) The war was a just and righteous one. If there was a war undertaken in the interests of civilization, humanity, commerce, and everything noble and good,it was the one in which our soldiers were now engage .3 in in South Africa Vernon was not their only IN presentative at the wareand if it continued there were otherA quite as willing to go and s icrifiee their lives for the sake of common humanity and the go)cl of the country. lie had great plc : sure in presetting Mr Vernon. on behalf of his fellow-workmen, with that testimony of their great respect for him. (Ap- plause.)—Private Vernon briefly responded. A vote of thanks having been accorded to Mr Naylor for making the presentation,the proceedings were brought to a close with the singing of the National Anthem.

div.head: WARRINGTON VOLUNTEERS AT ELAN DSLAAGTE. "One Huge Graveyard."
div.p: WARRINGTON VOLUNTEERS AT ELAN DSLAAGTE. "One Huge Graveyard."

Writing to his father who resides at 2, Mill-late, War- rington, Private Silt of the Ist VJlunteer B stcalion P.W.V. Sow h Lancashire regiment, now stationed at Elandsla-igte says :—There are thousands of our troops around this part of the country. Only to-day, a large body of cavalry paQsed hers on their way to Sundays River. Ainangst thm was Thorneyeroft's tierce, and a finer body of men I never saw in all my life before. It is rather musty smelling abut here at present. The huh not far fr )m camp are strewn with dead horses. We also fund dead Boers under our tents. The country round here is one huge graveyard. I suppose you have beard how our gallant regiment behaved in Spion Sop and the relief of Ladysmith. We are under the Aplandid general—Warren. He has proved himsrlf an able com- marvier and a brave soldier. ose of our poor chaps— William Blatkwood—has passed away. He was a nice fellow and well liked. He was the biggest and tallest young man ie the Volanteers.

div.head: Warrington Yeoman" Well and Happy."
div.p: A Warrington Yeoman" Well and Happy."

The following aro extracts from letters received May sth from Trooper I'. Davenport., son of Mr. Thomis Davenport, the Ackers. Latchford, who is now serving with t':e 220 d Cheshi-e Yeemanry in South Africa :—I wr-te to ler, you know I am in the lsnd of the living and am wog ard happy and hoot) everybody at bolus is the same. It is Sunday tc-day, but not much like Sunday either, but still it is all right. We are all as brown as berries, but all are in goad health at present, thank God. It goes very cold at night. We are about 3,000 strong driving the Boers before us, You would be sorry to see

how the Boars clear out the houses of Dutch people who won't fight for them. They take everything they can get in the way of eatables and destroy the rest. It is an awful sight to see. The Boer won't face us. We heard the other day they were close at hand, so we went wi:h all speed to find them, but they had just crossed the Orange River. I help to cook ante wait oa the officers- I have a man to look after my horse, or horses. as I ride all the fresh horses that come hero. I escorted the captain the other eley,and I picked and broke a horse for him, but it is a very bad country tor horses; they can't stand the heat. lam looking for- ward for a letter from home, for it seems ages since I had. one ; but we keep travelling farther away, and of course the letters have to follow. I have nn donbt you would be very surprised if you saw us all moun'ed. It is quite a wonderf al sight—gun carriage, ambulances, and everything. There is another thing would surprise you—to we us all gr ming beards and in austach,s. We have no time for shaving, and wash when we get th. chance- I shall come back as soon as this is over, and have a little more of Old E aglend. I believe this is a very nice country farther on,but I myself prefer Bogle Id for my borne, and many things besides. lam glad I came out here, because if lam spared it wi l be some- thing to look back upon, and I shall have an idea what things are like.—From your son, Tex.

div.head: Letter to the Rector from a South
div.p: Letter to the Rector from a South
Lancashire Sergeant.

The following letter has been received by the Rector of Warrington (the Rev. Canon Willis) from Sergeant Dr W A Ray, 3rd South Lancashire IL giment. "Coles berg Camp, Cape Colony, Bth April, 1901 Sir,—l take the liberty of addressing these few lines to you. Our regiment has been stationed in Colesberg Camp three weeks up to the time of writing. In the town there is a small English Church as Weil as a very large Dutch Reformed Church and a small Wetleyan Chapel. Ev sry Sunday since we have been stationed here I have made it a practice to att.nd the English Church, along with two or three other comradrs of the regiment. Oa me first visit to the church I was much struck with a hymn which was sung by the choir, and which has been sang each Sunday evening I have had the pleasure of going to church. I believe it has been written by some gen tleman in the Calmly, and has not b.ert heard in Eoglant It is set to a very popular tune, which you will see. Having mysslf been a member of toe old Parish Church, I should very much like if you would ' have it sung in your service by the old Parish Church choir. I have enclosed a copy of it, and I feel sure you will appreciate it. Sir, I dareray you will remember me when I explain lam the sergeant doctor of the South Lancashire Regiment Depot, Warrington ; was sta,'iened in. the Barracks at Warrington since April, 1893, until our regiment was embodied on the 13th of D camber, 1893, and which embarked for South Africa on the 16th January, 1900. I was for several years in charge of the baud in the depot, Warrington, which played far the Parish Church on Walking Day festival, and am very sorry that I shall not be able to be present this year ameng you, with my wife and family. Sir, we are now stationed at Colesberg, which is 100 miles from Bloemfontein, and 21 miles from Norval's Pont, Orange River, and we do not expect to move f 2 another week or two. General Roberts is gttling a tremendous force of troops in Bloemfontein, we think for the purpeffs of making one final, decisive blow, which we all hope will bring the campaign to a finish, or very nearly so. Of course, if they continue to boll out, and make us go on to Pretoria, it will prolong the war for at least another six months. Colesberg is 625 nines from Capetewn. The famous CO'ei Sep, which I have no doubt you have read about, is 2i miles from our camp, and I have climbed to the top ot it. It is 1.400 feet from. its base. oir artillery got one of their big guns to the top of it, and shelled the Boers, who were investing Colegbtrz. Our camp is pitched under Suffolk Hill, so called after the Suffolk lt,liment, who, you will remembsr, got a sur- prise, ween their colonel.adjet int,and two other officers were keled, along with 34 men. They are buried where they tell all in one grave The grave is half a mile from oar camp, out on the open veldt. lam pleased to say their last resting place has been looked after by the Berkshire Regiment, on the re-occupation of Colesberg by Gcneral Clement's column. They have erect•d a wooden cross at the head of the grave. I have lad my photo taken over the grave, and if you would like one I should be pleased to forward you one when I forward Mrs. Ray one. That will be as 80011 as I get them from the photographer's. fr3m Cape Town. Sir, I may tell you Mrs. Ray (my wife,) is still in the Barracks in Warrington, and I am sure she would be very pleised to see you any time you would wish to call en her. You could let her know if you would jigs one of the photos, and if so I would enclose it along with hen. I hay., written by this mail and told her that I was wririae to von. Sir, we have about 50 men down with dysentery. You never know the day you are going to be sick• All all right one day, sick the next. If I arrive home all safe I shall take the liberty of coming to see you. My 21 years' service is already completed, and it is my intention of settling down in Warrington. I hops that you will not think me forward in writing to you in the manner I have done, but while writing on one subject I Thought there would be no harm in telling you some- thing or our doings since we arrived in the country. I only hope sir, that you will have a glorious day for your scholars to walk on Walking Day—l suppose the lest Friday in Jene. I hope this will find you and your family enjoying good health.—l remain sir, year obedient servant, W. A. Ray, 3rd South, Llncashire Regiment."

div.head: Warrington Artilleryman's Interesting Adventures.
div.p: A Warrington Artilleryman's Interesting Adventures.

The following is a company of a letter written by Born. hardier F Lawless, to his mother. Mrs. E Plinstm, of 1 Orford lane, Warrington.-84h Battery R. H. Artillery,' Bloemfontien, April Bth, 1900.—Dear Mother and Father, —Just a few lines to say I am all right. I received your welcome letter of March 15th. I am glad to hear you are all well at home and my boy Harold is going to school,God bless him. Dear mother don't be alarmed if you see anything in the wipers about us for sometimes mistakes are made. We have been lighting our way every day for 76 miles up to here, where we are getting full rations. I am pleased to tell you no one was hurt in out Battery;oae of the enemy's shells dropped luckily for us, just behind our gun if it had been in front we should all have been put nut of mess. All the other batteries had killed and wounded except ours.so cheer up mother, I shall come through all right.l don't care how soon it is all over for it is weary work, we are up at three in the morning,and when daylight breaks we are on the enemy then we have to fight or chase them until nieht, then you are thankful to lay down on the ground until three again, then up and off. Lord Roberts gives teem no time when on the job. Certainly we have had mane narrow escapes but come out in the end. Many times I have dreamt I was at home and woke up sometimes to find myself wet through and my chums fast ash-ep b'- side me on the wet ground. I would give something if it was pesoille for a good breakfest of fried eggs and bacon, some good coffee, and nice white bread. It would go down ; but alas it is the old biscuit same as on board ship. We have been out twice since we first came here.We have had a couple of dab? at the enemy, and we have retired each time to Bloemfontein. Now about the papers : The Bloemfontein paper reported the Sete battery oone out to clear the country ; well, it was not correct, for we were here all the time. Another man in our battery went off in a hurry to send a few lines home, for he had just received a letter saying that they at home had read in the papers that he was killed. Mother, I don't wart to upset you with tales of the war. bat! have seen enough, killed end woun led. We were in that affair where 0 Battery were captured, U Batery all cut up ; none of Us were burg, but by the narrowest squeak we escsped captors. Next day we had to retire with their Porn Pomo rattling behind us. When we halted for the night, just underneath a few stones was one of our fellows that the Boers hsd taken prisoner, wounded I suppose, and had died and been hastily turied.l moved a stone and there were his hands across his breast ; I moved another and there were his feet. I don't know who he was, anyhow he had a pair of very fine blue socks on. He may have been an officer be the ' socks he wore and his hands wore quite clean not like ours dirty, for when on the march with the enemy about, we don't get tirnejto wash. I could not see his features for he had been shot through the head which was wrapped in a towel. We halted near a house which was used as an hospital during the fight, and it was horrible to see the wounded being brought in. The affair lasted over two days. One thing that surprised me,yras to see one fellow walk with the hele of a comrede for he had been shot clean through the head just below the temple and out at the other side, yet he could walk, and cocaine seine we pissed the place where a lot had ;wee berire, It m:kei yoe feel so sad and down when you see them. It makes you think of these at home who are waiting to welcome them, and then the pity of it to think toat they will never see them again. I don't mind the fighting, hut I don't like to see the graves of the dead, pour fellows ! I Well new for the humorous side. The Evxt night we had to do a quick march to another position, and going over some rough ground I lost my helmet. I jumped off the gun and ran back to try and find it, welt I looked for it in the dark until the guns were out of hearing and find- ing myself alone on the veldt, I had to set off to find the battery without it. Well we set off next morning. I had to wear my cap and going along the road back to Bloem- fontein the Major rode up to me and asked why I did net Come and askjeim for his soft hat—the officers wear them in cemp,they are a big orey wide a wake sort of thlng. " Well sir," I said, " I never dreamt of having the audacity to acme and ask you for your hat." " Oh "said he, " I would have lent it you, but it is packed away now. Anyhow go to my groom and ask him for a newspaper and make yourself a rough kind of sunshade." I thought it very kind. To-thy they have cent round for volunteers; for employment on the Im- perial Railway. They want tradesmen only. Land six others have had our names sent in so I will let you know how I go on. We are getting fat again here. They are paying us our money so we shall have a little money o come home wi,h for as dear as food is here we are totting it down,while we have the chance for God knows

we soon get thin when we get on the march. I must new close for I am writing this on tee floor by the light of a candle. Kiss my boy for see. I should like to s.e him. Give my love to brothers and sisters. Accept my hcst 1 ,vo and wishes from your loving son, FRED." P.B.—Or Mails got astray and came to he Modder. vve were then at Bops Drift. Then they were sent to Kimberley. I did expect one at Jacebsdat. When we got here I was so thankful to receive it ; if you had seen the rush when someone shouted "Roll up for your letters," you would have wept with joy. Tommy's money soon goes as you will see, for we pay cheese 2s 61 lb ; 21b loaf ls ; small tin of golden syrup 24 61; tin of nutter 5s ; tin preserves 3 61; herrings Is each; bottle of herb beer 3 eggs 23 ; tin of condensed milk 13 61 and 23 ; lib ot meal is ; sugar is lb.; moderate prices for limited pockets. —FRED.

div.head: An Irishman's Patriotism.
div.p: An Irishman's Patriotism.

At the Warrin!ton Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. F. Monks and other magistriites, Michael HennesFi a labourer, was charged with hiving 'peen druLk aryl disorderly in Buttermarket-Ptreet at twenty minutes to eight on Sunday night.—P.C. Fish stated that he saw defendant in company with his brother. He was drunk and was jostling people. Witness cautioned him, and asked him to go away s .veral time!. He refused to en and was taken into custody. He became rough, and Sergeant 13,11 assisted witness to take him to the Police Stetion.—Defendant said he hoped the magistrates would be lenient. He was extremely sorry for what hnd occurred. On Sunday evening there was a rumour that Mafeking had been relieved, and he became excited and get drunk. He was too jubilant. If they would give him a ch ince he promised faithfully from the bottom of his heart that he would not touch another drop of drinli until Field-Marshal Roberts had attained the height of his ambilon aryl put the Union Jack together with the shamrock over Krug(T's resideace in Pretoria. (Laugh- ter.) If h. (defendant) had done anything to the officer lie humbly apologized. It was only patriotism. (Laughter.)—The Cnairm. an : We will not fine you the costs on account of your nationality. Your countrymen have done good work in South Africa. You will be fined sr.—Defendant: Thank you. lam extremely obliged to you.

div.head: Fort at Johannesburg.
div.p: The Fort at Johannesburg.

Unlike Pretoria, which lies in a narrow cu-shaped valiey, Johannestur,g is built on the a!ope of toe bare treeless downs , hich constitute the Witwatersrand. The fort has been erected on the crest of the bill, and domin itea the whole of the town which lie' outstretched beneath it. It a!so commands the level summit of the hill on both sides to the right and left, and a distance of a mile to a mile and a halt of level grouA at the back which exteac's between it and where the hillside breaks abruptly away into a valley lying nearly a thousand feet below. It is an ideal position for a fort, for it would be impoasib:o for an enemy to approach it unobserved, or, it the houses in its immediate vicinity were destroyed, to obtain cover whilst making an attack. the walls of the fort consist of sloping banks of earth about 30 feet in height, crowned en the top by an embrasured parapet. Inside these etrth binks are bomb-proof concrete chambers for the men to live in, and within the gaol is a well, so that tOore is no danger of a scarcity of water. At the time of our visit he fort was only just finished, and the guns had not yet arrived I was told they were on their way out, and were expected in about a month's time, and I was shown both where the big guns were to be placed, and also the Maxims for enfilading the glacis. Thii was in January 1898 —just two years after the rd i l—and that the fort shohd have been then still uncompleted goes some way to prove that at any rate the more exten- sive of the Transvaal armaments wire suivequen*, and not anterior, to the Raid —" From " From the Boer .Republics," in the " Cornhill Magazine " for May.

div.head: MILITARY NOTES.
div.p: MILITARY NOTES.

Serp„eant Major John McCullough, serving at Warrington as Sergeant Major of the Bth tcegi- mental Diitrict, has been promoted to a commission as quarter-master with the honorary rank of Lieut. for duty as quarter-master ef tae 6th battalion, Liverpool Regiment, lately embodied at Warring- ton for service in Ireland. Mr. McCullough is well- known at Warrington and is a smart soldier who has well earned his commission. Be became Ser- geant Major of the d3pbt of the Liverpool Regiment in Dscember 1898 in succession to Mr. Bailey who was then promoted quarter-master of the .5;.-,h and 6th battalions Liveroeol Regiment with heni guar- ttrs at Warrington but under the new arrangement each ot these battalions will have a quarter-master instead of as hitherto there being one quarter- master for the two battalions.
Captain Greenway has been promotei major in the Liverpool Regiment. He joined the corps in 1884 from the Bedfordshire Militia and was at one time serving at Warrington with the depeit com- panies, _

sir. J. W. Allen who formerly held a commission in the 6th Battalion Liverpool Regiment with headquarters at Warrington has been re-appointe ' captain and has taken over command of a company in the corps. Captain Allen obtained his first com- mission in the old 2nd Royal Lancashire Militia in May, 1888, and was promoted captain in July,lB9o He resigned his commission only a short time ago. Captain Crosfield of the Ist Volunteer Battalion South Lancashire Regiment with head qnarters at Warrington having joined the Imperial Yeomanry has been formally seconded from his Volunteer Battalion in which he became Captain last January. There are now vacancies for two captains in this corps to fill the vacancies caused by the seconding of the officer above named an-I also cf Ctptain Appleton, who is now in command of the Volunteer Company attached to the Ist Battalion South Lanca- shire Regiment in South Africa.

Ten n-on-commissicued officers have been given commissions as Second Lieutenants for services in the South African campaign. One of the ten —Corporal Norman Victor Stoddard of the Gordon Highlanders, has been appointed Second Lieutenant in the Liverpool Regiment and joins the Ist battalion in Natal. Second Lieutenant &olden, we understand servel with the 2nd battalion: Gor- don Highlanders during the defence of Ladysmith in which defence the Ist battalion Liverpool Regi- ment also participated.

Second Lieutenant Douglas Stephen of the 3rd battalion South Lancashire Regiment with head- quarters at Warrington, has been given a commis- sion in the brigade of Guards becoming Lieutenant in the Grenadier Guards. Mr. Stephen who joined the local militia battalion last January on transfer from another corps will it is expected, join the 2nd battalion.

div.head: THEFT BY A HOMELESS LAD.
div.p: THEFT BY A HOMELESS LAD.

At the Warrington Police Cilift on Thursday morn- ing, before Alderman Satton (in the chair) and Mr. fieph?rd, John Darbyehire (16), of no settled abode,was charged with stealing from the stables of the Crown Inn yard, off Queen-Et., between nine o'clock on Wednesday morning and seven o'clock the same evening, a horse's bit, valued at 2i., the property of Robert Robinson.— He pleaded guilty.—Superintendent Monaghan stated that the prosecutor was a draper living at St. Helens and attended the Warrington market on Wednesdays. On Wednesday morning he drove to Warrinaton,and put his horse and cart up at the Crown Inn,off QuPen-street. At seven o'clock in the evening Detective Forster was in Mersey-street and met the prisoner with the bit in his pocket. He questioned him and brought him to the Police Station. Inquiries were made and it was found that the bit had been stolen from the bridle belonging to the prosecutor, and was afterwards identifiNi by him. Pr;soner had told him that he came from Manchester,and that he went about the country. He also said that he had been in Knutsford and Manchester prisons for various offmc.s.—ln reply to the Chairman prisoner said he had a father, who was living with his aunt. Ile had no mother.—He was committed to pi ison for a month with hard labour.
Personal.

The Rev. W R Hartwright, curate of Padgate and Orford, has been offered and has accepted the living of Pitminster,near Taunton, the patron of which is the Rev. A Elton, of Widworthy Court, flonion. Mr. Hartwright has been in this district for nearly seven years and the news of his departure will be received with regret.
Strike of Slipper Makers.
At a meeting of the•Warrington Filesmiths' A- sociation held on Tnesday evening it was decided to make a grant of .E 2 to assist the Jewish slipper makers of Leeds, who are out on strike.

AULD LANG SYNE. Now when you sit in ease at home, Remember those afar; Those gallant lads across the foam, Who are fighting at the war. For Auld Lang Syne, my boys, or the sake of Auld Lang Syne, You all can share their cares, and joys, As you did in Auld Lang Syne. There English, Irish, Scotch and Welsh, Are fighting at the front, Fighting together for one cause, Not one of them will funk. Then raise a cheer for Bobs and Co., That gallant fighting line, And may they win, where e'er they:go, As they did in Auld Lang Syne. And when we think of those who're gone, And the loved ones who do pine, Let us then cheer them, all alone, For the sake of Auld Lang Syne. And give your share of money, do, And drop a word that's kind, Your actions you will never rue, When you think of Auld Lang Syne. We know our chaps will do right well, Whilst fighting for their Queen, They chance their lives mid shot and shell, As they did in Auld Lang Syne. So let us cheer, the rank and file, The noble fighting line, Those plucky men, who for us toil, As they did in Auld Lang Syne. G.H.W.S.
